entries.title: Celia Paul on Her Memoir, Life, and Art
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In this episode of Private Life, Celia Paul joins Jarrett Earnest for a conversation about her art, writing, and life. Paul reflects on self-portraiture, grief, her relationship with Lucien Freud, and the painting La Tempesta by Giorgione, which figures prominently in her new memoir, Objects of Desire: An Artist in Venice, published this month by New York Review Books.  

Celia Paul is a British painter based in London. She studied at the Slade School of Fine Art from 1976 to 1981. Her work is in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the British Museum, and the National Portrait Gallery in London. Gladstone Gallery presented a solo exhibition of Paul’s work titled Innervisions in the spring of 2026. A solo show, Celia Paul: Objects of Desire, is now open at Victoria Miro Venice. She is also the author of Self Portrait (2020) and Letters to Gwen John (2022), both published by NYRB.

You can find Objects of Desire and other books by Celia Paul at nyrb.com or at your favorite bookseller.

entries.title: The Struggle Has Begun

entries.content:
With so many horrors to choose from—the lies and broken promises; the violence, sadism, and vengefulness; the extortion, graft, and grift; the open contempt for the laws, stated ideals, and noncriminal residents of the country that the current administration was elected to steward—an exasperated public had no need to wrack its brains over what issues to vote on, and simply returned a resounding Enough.

As the results came in, the great national exhalation expressed the relief of a dreamer when the parachute finally opens after all. But the dream itself senses the alligator swamp below, and stretching beyond it burned bridges, sacked storehouses, gutted libraries, bombed-out schools, and fields piled high with corpses. The interregnum between now and January promises months of held breath.

One area of concern, obviously, is our fanciful president. How much damage will he effect before, cornered and raging, he can be hauled off the main stage? And how much of that damage will be intentional, and how much accidental—a cigarette butt casually dropped into a dry forest? A second worry is the thugs the president is splashing around into ever more prominent positions, most threateningly the spectacularly vile Stephen Miller as chief of staff, and most comically (or maybe most depressingly) the mixed-martial-arts impresario Dana White, who declined Trump’s half-hearted invitation to serve as press secretary. A third concern are the sinister “intellectuals” of the MAGA movement—the authors, for instance of Project 2025, the shadowy white supremacist jurists, “educators,” and tactics geeks. They are dogged, crafty, and resourceful, and they endure.

But those concerns are specific to the Republican Party—and not all of it, at that. If January comes without some new, astoundingly irrational and destructive foreign adventure, or new legislation that’s a death knell to the environment, or a new ghoul seated on the Supreme Court, or a total economic collapse, it will be the Democratic Party and individual Democratic lawmakers who are floodlit as the serious, the true engines of anxiety production. The question is already everywhere: Will the Democrats seize the opportunity—no, the mandate!—they’ve been given, to create from the wreckage a model for a working society in the form of a constitutional democracy, or will they simply modify the cruel policies of the Trump years and return to a lethal status quo? The struggle has begun, as evidenced in flurries of emails, endless articles, calls for meetings, chatter everywhere, and, concretely, in the sudden, unexpected possibility of Chuck Schumer being replaced in January as the Senate majority leader by Chris Van Hollen.

Voters were polled right after voting day. Polling questions are broad approximations, and respondents say what they say, but results probably yield some information. Large numbers said they voted Democrat because of “the cost of living.” And few would argue that increased and unpredictable expenses have been a trivial concern. But a more revealing reason cited by a very large number of voters was “corruption.”

The word cannot be shorn of its medical associations. It has a biblical ring of affliction and degradation. It suggests uncontainable illness and decay of the entire body politic itself—illness it might be impossible to protect oneself against. It’s one thing if a larcenous politician sticks his hand in your pocket and grabs your wallet—that’s unpleasant enough. But what’s a great deal more unpleasant than the actual loss is the sensation of loss—the sensation that you’ve been duped, that you’ve been victimized, that you’ve failed to protect something—and the very intense subsequent sensations of helplessness and shame (symptoms of a corrupted state) have been intensified exponentially, as we learn, daily, over and over, what’s being done to the environment in the name of profits, what’s being done to the ideal of a nation of laws in the service of personal gain—and, especially, what’s being done to individuals, to families, to children, by means of kidnapping, illegal incarceration, illegal deportation, and flat-out disappearings, in illustration of the will and ability of those holding the reins to exercise unconstrained and capricious power.

While so many of us have been paralyzed in the face of these assaults on our rights, our well-being, our neighbors, there have been others who have acted in defiance, who have spoken out loudly. A number of journalists have continued to record abominations. Our hopes have hung on the courage of those who resist, some of whom, as we know, have paid the ultimate price. The newly elected have been elected largely to listen to the voices of those courageous people, and follow their lead in protecting the interests of everyone. It’s for them now to show courage and to justify our provisional faith in them. The roles are clear. The new lawmakers have been charged with preparing for a sustainable republic that represents the whole variety of people who live in our country and people who come to it with hope. And we, their constituents, must keep insisting that they do. Whether we succeed or fail to rectify the unspeakable mess we’re in, we succeed or fail together.

entries.content:
On September 7, 2025, supporters of Jair Bolsonaro marked Brazil’s Independence Day by carrying a giant American flag—“the size of a basketball court,” the New York Times journalist Jack Nicas noted with astonishment—down Avenida Paulista in São Paulo. The former president was then under trial for an attempted coup d’état that included a plot to assassinate President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (known as Lula), Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, and the federal Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes. (The conspiracy even had a name—“Green and Yellow Dagger”—and a written plan printed at the Palácio do Planalto by a senior member of the administration.) Donald Trump had lately come to Bolsonaro’s defense, and the protesters waving the US flag that day were showing their appreciation. They called themselves “patriots.”

It was a curious choice of word. Just a month earlier, citing what he called the “witch hunt” against Bolsonaro and falsely insinuating that the US was suffering losses in its trade relationship with Brazil, Trump had imposed a 50 percent tariff on Brazilian goods. The new levies were poised to harm the country’s economy, and Brazilian exports indeed contracted right after they went into effect.

But for some far-right Brazilians, the backlash prompted by the tariffs did little to dim their support for Trump. For months Paulo Figueiredo, grandson of Brazil’s last dictator, and Jair’s son Eduardo Bolsonaro had been pressuring the US to protect Jair from imminent arrest by punishing Brazilian Supreme Court justices for prosecuting him. Alongside the tariffs, Trump invoked the Global Magnitsky Act to sanction Justice Moraes, who was presiding over Bolsonaro’s trial. Yet neither the economic offensive nor the sanctions achieved their goal. The former president was convicted and imprisoned along with high-ranking military figures involved in the plot, and the effects of the tariffs were limited: exports to the US accounted for less than 2 percent of Brazil’s GDP, and the losses were soon outweighed by an increase in soy exports to China.

That disappointing outcome did not prevent the “patriots” from continuing to appeal to the United States. Indeed their rhetoric grew still more sinister. In 2026, during a major demonstration backing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro—Jair’s eldest son—in his effort to unseat Lula in this fall’s Brazilian general elections, a group of protesters displayed a white, inflatable missile bearing the words TRUMP NUKE BRAZIL.

That slogan distilled a worldview that has spread across Brazil’s right since Trump’s return to power. America is a nation that has “made it”: strong, sovereign, generous to those who work hard, and, under Trump, devoted to God, family, and guns, with communism as its sworn enemy. Such a country is to be revered, copied, and saluted. Bolsonaro himself, a retired captain of the Brazilian army, saluted the American flag twice: in October 2017, as a presidential candidate addressing supporters in Deerfield Beach, Florida, amid chants of “USA! USA!”; and in May 2019, as president, at a business luncheon in Dallas, where he also reworked his campaign slogan into “Brazil and the United States above everything.” Anyone who stands in Trump’s way, Brazil included, risks being “nuked” or seized like Nicolás Maduro. In August the Republican congressman Carlos Gimenez posted a doctored image of Lula in the place of the captured Venezuelan leader, captioned “what awaits him.” Eduardo Bolsonaro promptly reposted it. How did the Brazilian far right end up wanting to submit to the US so completely?

Ten years earlier, on October 22, 2016, the third edition of the Liberty and Democracy Forum, a conference dedicated to free-market ideas, took place in São Paulo. The first panel, titled “The Role of the State in the Twenty-First Century,” featured Fábio Ostermann, a cofounder of the Free Brazil Movement (MBL), Senator Ana Amélia Lemos, and Jair Bolsonaro, at the time a federal deputy representing Rio de Janeiro. The discussion was moderated by Hélio Beltrão, president of the Mises Institute Brazil.

At the time I was working on my doctoral thesis on the emergence of a “new right” in Brazil, and I attended the event accompanied by one of my primary informants, Bernardo Santoro. As director of the free-market Liberal Institute, Santoro had been actively involved in Flávio Bolsonaro’s unsuccessful campaign for mayor of Rio de Janeiro, a race that had concluded just weeks earlier. When we got to the venue Ostermann, whom I had interviewed before, spotted us and confronted Santoro about the politics of Ostermann’s co-panelist. How, he asked, could a free-market advocate like Santoro support a dictator like Bolsonaro?1

At the time it was common for young libertarians to feel a strong aversion toward Jair Bolsonaro. After all, the twenty-year military dictatorship (1964–1985) under which he served as an officer was statist and authoritarian (with the exception of the first three years, when the economically liberal Castelo Branco was president)—a regime that would horrify any remotely consistent libertarian. Bolsonaro took that authoritarian, reactionary politics even further: in 1999, while serving as a federal deputy, he advocated on television for the closure of Congress and the killing of “some 30,000 people, starting with Fernando Henrique Cardoso,” the country’s president at the time. In 2011 he stated that he would rather his son die in an accident than come out as gay; three years later he argued that men should earn more than women because they do not get pregnant.

In 2016 Brazilian free-market campaigners were still embarrassed to be associated with the right, precisely because of the legacy of the military dictatorship. Santoro himself did not identify as a right-winger; in his view, for Brazil’s libertarians to ally with conservative—or even reactionary—politicians like Jair Bolsonaro was a tactical move rather than a gesture of deep ideological affinity. A radical program of privatization and economic liberalization was, after all, unpopular in the country, whereas Bolsonaro’s brand of right-wing thought—which railed against “gender ideology” and a so-called “gay kit” supposedly handed out to children in public schools—was winning a growing grassroots following among voters who saw Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT) as corrupt, morally depraved, and committed to rewarding idleness rather than hard work. Repeatedly in our conversations Santoro emphasized that conservatism was the means; free-market liberalism was the end.

The benefits of this alliance were mutual. It was Bolsonaro’s decision to take direction from the economist Paulo Guedes that made him palatable to Brazil’s financial elites. A highly regarded economist in libertarian circles who had emerged from among the cohort of “Chicago Boys” in the 1970s and later became Bolsonaro’s minister of the economy, Guedes worked diligently between 2017 and 2018 to assure concerned Brazilian financial elites that Bolsonaro had “become a different animal.” The candidate, he argued, had accepted the rules of the democratic game and an economic agenda centered on liberalization, as the journalist Malu Gaspar noted in the Brazilian monthly piauí. Yet it did not take long, as Gaspar also pointed out, for Guedes to get swallowed up by the very creature he had promised to “tame.”

For some time I hesitated to label Bolsonaro’s political movement fascism. Scholars have long debated whether the word technically applies to the Brazilian military regime from which his political convictions emerged. In 1969 the dependency theorist Theotonio dos Santos called the dictatorship a form of “dependent fascism,” by which he meant that it was a fascism with no national project it could actually carry out, because the regimes that promoted it were structurally subordinate to the very foreign interests—multinational capital and imperial powers—that in theory it should have opposed. The nationalist Hélio Jaguaribe, meanwhile, called it “colonial fascism,” arguing that the dictatorship had stifled any authentic nationalism and kept Brazil a virtual colony. But intellectuals such as Juan Linz, Guillermo O’Donnell, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, and Atilio Borón argued that several aspects of the dictatorship made the parallel with European fascism misleading in the first place.

Historical fascism mobilized the masses through a “party-movement.” The Brazilian dictatorship, by contrast, did the opposite: it demobilized and excluded popular sectors. It was the military establishment, not a political party, that held power, allowing only a “permitted” opposition that served as a democratic veneer for the regime.

Nor did the regime have charismatic leaders; generals took turns in office. João Figueiredo, Brazil’s last dictator, once declared that he preferred “the smell of horses” to “the smell of the people.” Though there was a movement of far-right Brazilian thinkers, known as “integralists,” who explicitly attached themselves to historical fascism, they and their primary leader, Plínio Salgado, were merely junior partners to the regime. For this reason most scholars of the Brazilian military dictatorship define it as a form of authoritarianism rooted in repression, devoid of any mass movement that would make it a style of fascism.

As Bolsonaro rose to power, it was precisely this element—the support of the masses—that his administration gained. His most energetic backing came from conservative evangelical pastors, self-employed workers, and aspiring entrepreneurs. As the anthropologist Rosana Pinheiro-Machado describes, these segments have come to form a new aspirational class, driven by anger toward a state they consider not just corrupt but blind to their interests and indifferent to their fate. A newly decentralized and Internet-powered mass party also emerged—what Marcos Nobre and researchers at the Brazilian Center of Analysis and Planning (CEBRAP) have called the “Bolsonarista Digital Party.” The far-right legislators Nikolas Ferreira and Cleitinho, with their millions of followers, represent this entity in its purest form: a network of digital-native politicians who use their fame and platforms to command loyalty, effectively parasitizing traditional parties. This year Ferreira was reelected to Congress with more than three million votes, the largest tally for a federal deputy in Brazil’s history, while Cleitinho, a senator, was elected governor of Minas Gerais in the first round.

And yet Bolsonaro’s government lacked the repressive apparatus of the military dictatorship. Like the military regime, it singled out the Supreme Court for attack—Bolsonaro hurled insults at justices and declared in 2021 that he would no longer comply with their decisions—and questioned the validity of electronic voting machines in rhetoric that echoed the dictatorship’s manipulation of electoral rules. Naturally it also needed a reincarnated “communist” enemy, which it found in the PT, the powerful left party established in 1980, toward the end of the dictatorship. But Bolsonaro’s presidency stopped short of using state power to detain, imprison, and murder its enemies en masse. Instead violence spread in a diffuse manner: access to firearms, for instance, was expanded under the guise of allowing “upstanding citizens” to defend themselves.

The military dictatorship, in other words, featured repression without mass mobilization, whereas Bolsonaro’s rule involved mass mobilization without a state-run repressive apparatus. It did, however, galvanize a persistent movement that aligned with the historian Robert Paxton’s view of fascism as a process that unfolds in stages, from the founding of an organized political formation to its rooting in political life, its alliance with conservative elites, and, sometimes, the conquest of the state. Most fascist movements, like the Ku Klux Klan, never got that far but were no less fascist for it. Yet what form of Brazilian fascism could include waving an American flag the size of a basketball court, or calling for a nuclear strike against one’s own nation?

To understand this strange development, it may seem natural to return to the theories of “dependent” and “colonial” fascism developed in the late 1960s by thinkers such as Dos Santos and Jaguaribe. Both theorists described a structural, imposed domination: Brazil, they argued, was forced to depend on a world capitalist system with its center in the United States. Under the dictatorship, that dependence was real. When the Federal Reserve sent interest rates soaring in 1979, Brazil’s debts soon became unpayable, forcing the country into the arms of the IMF and ushering in a “lost decade” of stagnation and hyperinflation. Yet this dependence on Washington was mediated by creditors and the IMF rather than openly embraced.

Today the picture is different. Brazil may indeed occupy a subordinate economic position within the international system, but that position is quite clearly not the one of dependency to which it was consigned decades ago. The limited impact of Trump’s 50 percent tariff on Brazilian goods showed how autonomous the country’s economic position has become. Brazil holds more than $300 billion in reserves, and it has much of what the world wants, from rare earths to clean energy—resources that it can leverage in negotiations with a variety of nations, rather than remaining beholden to the US. China has been its largest trading partner since 2009. None of this stopped Flávio Bolsonaro, at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Texas this past March, from offering his country up anyway: “Brazil is America’s solution,” he declared, “to break independence on China for critical minerals, especially rare-earth elements.”

A more persuasive explanation for such rhetoric can be found in an interview that the military general and former UN peacekeeping commander Santos Cruz, who served briefly as a minister in Bolsonaro’s administration, gave last month to the journalist Bruno Torturra. At a certain point the exchange turned to how Bolsonaro’s allies had cheered Trump’s tariffs and urged Washington to punish Brazil’s Supreme Court justices. “Seeking external support, in the way it was done, is absurd,” Cruz said.

It is, in fact, an assault on Brazil’s sovereignty…. It is voluntary submission. Seeking outside interference is treason…. I consider myself a man of the right; but what this is—this isn’t “the right.” This is nothing more than a swindle.

Instead of “dependency fascism,” we might say that the contemporary Brazilian right is under the influence of “submission fascism.” Here dependence on a more powerful foreign country is not an inescapable structural condition but a “voluntary” object of desire, deliberately sought for the sake of defeating an internal enemy. In Brazil, those who beseech the US to undermine the country’s institutions and Lula’s government hope it will help them finally defeat the PT, free Jair Bolsonaro, and clear his way back to power. This choice to submit originates not just from the elites—as Jaguaribe once suggested—but also from a popular base. It is a choice made during a time of peace and democracy, rather than under the duress of war or the threat of imminent attack.

At first this desire for submission was directed toward an internal protector. In 2022 the so-called “patriots” sought to have the armed forces intervene via a coup d’état to “save” Brazil from another Workers’ Party administration, which they characterized as a “left-wing dictatorship.” As the sociologist Jonas Medeiros has described, for months they camped out near military barracks, carrying signs and chanting with religious fervor: “Armed Forces, save Brazil!” When the military failed to heed their call, the “patriots” took matters into their own hands, culminating in the ransacking of the seats of the three branches of government on January 8, 2023.

Immediately following Trump’s reelection, the imagery of salvation shifted. In 2025 signs held by “patriots” at protests read “SOS Trump” and “Help me.” The desire remained for a “moderating power” that could ensure the nation’s salvation; what changed was who would provide that salvation, and how.

If the traditional right, as represented by figures like Santos Cruz, was aghast at the prospect of treating Trump as Brazil’s savior, the response from the “new right” was more muted. Libertarians like Santoro and Guedes may have begun supporting Bolsonaro as a tactic to advance a free-market agenda, but now they have little of substance to say about his movement’s open submission to Trump, which flies in the face of their stated principles. From a neoliberal point of view, as Santoro himself has implied, it makes no sense for Brazil to commit its rare earths to the US instead of selling them to the highest bidder. Why haven’t they put up a fight?

The answer to that question lies elsewhere in the content of the economic thought they promoted. By importing radical libertarian ideas, the Brazilian new right also imported a view of the international system that was designed to curtail the economic sovereignty of peripheral nations like Brazil. As Quinn Slobodian has argued, free-market ideologues like Ludwig von Mises were willing to accept the political independence of former colonies and peripheral countries—but not their right to control their own resources or nationalize companies.2 The rights of capital were always to be prioritized over the rights of workers in the periphery. These peripheral nations could be “free,” provided they did not use that freedom to challenge foreign capital. When Trump abandoned free-market neoliberalism in favor of an “America First” agenda characterized by heavy tariffs, sanctions, and disputes over rare-earth minerals, the new right and its peripheral-nation libertarians found themselves without the vocabulary to defend their own national interests.

Renan Santos, a leader of the Free Brazil Movement, was one of the few to recognize this danger. As a presidential candidate in the 2026 elections, he openly criticized the Bolsonarista movement’s subservience to Trump and proposed pivoting instead toward a right-wing developmentalist nationalism. Brazil, in his view, ought to treat its rare earths as leverage rather than as a gift, suspending deals until the minerals could be processed at home, and bargaining hard with Washington, Tokyo, and Europe for technology and investment. Trump, he said, “only knows how to deal with people who negotiate hard with him.”

These dynamics loomed large over the election earlier this fall. Voters I interviewed during the campaign who intended to cast their ballots for Flávio Bolsonaro followed the “patriots” in choosing to submit to the US, but on somewhat different grounds. Only by joining the “shield of the Americas,” they argued, could Brazil finally put a stop to urban crime and rein in its criminal factions.

Among the elites, Flávio Bolsonaro’s most enthusiastic backers were the cattle ranchers and soybean growers of the Green and Yellow Brazil Movement. The anthropologist Caio Pompeia identifies this movement with the most politically extreme wing of Brazilian agribusiness—what he calls “agri-Bolsonaristas.”3 Its leaders dispute climate science, have called for abolishing the Environment Ministry and weakening the Forest Code, and want Indigenous lands opened to farming. They have some reason to be wary of Trump, but his second-term trade wars have so far done them more good than ill: largely unaffected by the US’s aggressive tariff hikes on Brazil’s own goods, they profited handsomely when China replaced American soy with Brazilian soy. Seeking high-risk, short-term economic gains, they demand the freedom to clear-cut forests and encroach upon protected or demarcated lands in the Amazon and other biomes.

As for the financial elites, they would have preferred São Paulo Governor Tarcísio de Freitas; they supported Flávio Bolsonaro only because they had no other choice. To appease them, after finishing the first round of the election ahead of Lula, with a lead of more than two million votes, Flávio openly proposed an economic program inspired by that of Javier Milei, much to the delight of the fringe libertarians. But as Santoro warned in 2016, libertarianism is inherently unpopular among much of the electorate. Flávio’s choice to loudly and clearly announce his intended economic agenda—including cutting around 250 billion reais (more than $44 billion) from public spending and requiring “free” negotiation between employers and employees—surely contributed to his loss in the election’s second round.

The first-round votes, which delivered a majority to pro-Bolsonaro senators and raised the prospect of gaining control over the Supreme Federal Court, also emboldened Flávio. Soon he started openly stating that he wished to amend the Constitution in order to “re-democratize the country,” a claim that many voters interpreted—correctly—as a sign that he would have both the legislative and the judicial branches in his pocket. A number of Brazilians who until then had been undecided or had abstained in the first round were gripped by panic. In one interview I conducted during the campaign, a voter gave voice to this shared understanding that a Flávio administration would dismantle social and labor rights:

What’s going to happen is that they’ll impose a dictatorship in Brazil, with only his family in power. The Senate is his; everyone there is already on his side. Flávio has carte blanche to do whatever he wants—and impeachment is off the table; with this Senate, it’s just not possible. And this whole idea of ​​hourly wages and negotiating directly with one’s boss—it’s going to be a pro-business government.

In just three weeks, Lula gained over 10 million new votes, ultimately winning by a margin of 4.4 million. As the sociologist Thais Pavez remarked to me, invoking Walter Benjamin, the majority of Brazilians pulled the emergency brake just in time.

But the train has not yet come to a complete stop; the “America First, Brazil Last” project remains alive. Three days after the election Flávio Bolsonaro fled to the US and released a letter declaring himself the true president of Brazil. Soon afterward, I interviewed voters who had backed Lula only in the runoff out of fear. The women spoke of suspicion. “Trump gave him political shelter,” one told me. “I don’t rule out that he’s planning something with Flávio. I saw that one of his aides helped Flávio escape. It makes you wary.” The men, without being prompted, spoke of sovereignty. “If Flávio had won, he would have handed the rare earths to Trump,” one said. “Brazil would have become America’s backyard.”

entries.title: When Democrats Became the Populists
entries.summary: The sixth episode of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole was taped live, with a remote audience, a week after the midterms dealt a resounding rebuke to the Trump administration and a huge congressional victory to the Democrats. Rhodes and Taylor offer their interpretations of the election results and talk about what the Democrats in Congress will […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
The sixth episode of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole was taped live, with a remote audience, a week after the midterms dealt a resounding rebuke to the Trump administration and a huge congressional victory to the Democrats. Rhodes and Taylor offer their interpretations of the election results and talk about what the Democrats in Congress will need to do in order to avoid squandering this historic opportunity: govern as populists and pass legislation supported by a great majority of Americans, like ending the war in Iran, regulating AI and data center construction, and organizing around Medicare for All.

Ben Rhodes is a writer and the cochair of National Security Action, an advocacy group based in Washington, D.C. He was the Deputy National Security Adviser for Strategic Communications and Speechwriting under President Obama from 2009 to 2017 and has been contributing to The New York Review since 2023. His latest book, All We Say: The Battle for American Identity, was published earlier this year.

Astra Taylor is a documentary filmmaker, political organizer, and writer who has contributed to the Review since 2020. Her latest film is What Is Democracy? (2018) and her latest book, End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World,was cowritten with Naomi Klein and published earlier this year.

entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

Tally Brown “graced stages of all sizes and delighted audiences of all types,” Melissa Anderson writes in our November 19, 2026, issue. As seen in Rosa von Praunheim’s 1979 documentary Tally Brown, New York, she was an “indelible figure: short and rotund, outrageously bewigged,” with “gapped teeth and mile-long false eyelashes.” Anderson’s essay, occasioned by a recent restoration of the film, conveys Brown’s contagious sense of pride in her hedonism, her work, and above all her hometown, both the scrappy New York of her youth and the queer nightlife in the city where she spent much of her adulthood.

Anderson has been a film critic for more than two decades. Her reviews are a first port of call for many moviegoers upon leaving the theater: lively, dense with reference, and, it seems, always correct. For nine years Anderson was the film editor and lead film critic at 4Columns; though the website stopped publishing earlier this year, her vast archive there is still available online, full of her characteristically sharp, tightly woven opinions on contemporary movies and repertory screenings, with occasional wide-ranging essays on, for example, Jane Fonda in the 1970s. (Her book The Hunger collects over a decade of her film writing.) She was the film editor at Time Out New York and the senior film critic at the Village Voice and is currently a columnist at Film Comment. For many years she wrote about film for Artforum, and she is a regular contributor to Bookforum. Her monograph on David Lynch’s Inland Empire was published in 2021. Over email this week she tried to convince me that there’s no point in being alarmist about the fate of cinema.

Nawal Arjini: You are a great chronicler of the filmic and literary representations of New York’s twentieth-century queer underbelly. As the city has gotten “cleaner and shinier,” as you write, and as queer life has increasingly entered the mainstream, where in New York do you see these scenes persist, or where are new ones beginning?

Melissa Anderson: When I moved to New York, in 1996, I spent countless hours in Manhattan dyke bars and clubs, which were then flourishing: Meow Mix (later to relocate to Brooklyn and become Cattyshack), Crazy Nanny’s, the Cubbyhole, Rubyfruit, and Henrietta Hudson, among others. Of these stalwarts, only the Cubbyhole and Henrietta’s remain (and Ginger’s, in Brooklyn, which opened in 2000). I am no longer a habitué, but I always have a good time during my occasional visits. I am also no longer young and not as much of a nocturnal creature as I once was, with an instinct for where things are happening. But I am fortunate to be close friends with three lesbians who are about thirty years my junior—they are my “youth spies,” to use John Waters’s term, and they keep me au courant. Sometimes, we make discoveries together: two months ago, after a screening we all attended at e-flux, we happened upon a fabulous lesbian sports bar in Clinton Hill, Athena Keke’s. I aim to be like Tally Brown, who was a lifelong New Yorker and loved the city with a tremendous passion but abhorred nostalgia. She never thought that the city was better, was at its peak, when she was in her twenties and thirties. She knew the city was constantly reborn and reenergized by young people.

You spent many years as the film editor and critic at 4Columns, an arts site with firm constraints—a thousand words, every week. Your previous work at Time Out also involved even more brutal space restrictions; did having to condense your thoughts this way shape the way you think about movies, or writing? And how did it feel to write in a relatively unconstrained fashion for us?

How I think about a particular movie has never been affected by word count, which, in the twenty-plus years I’ve been a film critic, has typically ranged between 200 and 1,200 words. And no matter the length of the piece, I always want a robust intro and outro, so I will spend too much time fussing over ledes and kickers. But the more words I have, the more space I can devote to widening the discussion, expounding on certain points, or, in the case of writing about an older film, providing more historical background. Thus, for the New York Review piece on Tally Brown, New York, I could devote some time to talking about the career of Rosa von Praunheim, the documentary’s German director, and his fascination with NYC.

A recent essay in n+1 argued that the “intellectual situation” is one of literary necrophilia: all anyone is reading these days are old books, partly because it’s all anyone is publishing. Repertory screening is not a new feature of cinematic culture, especially in New York, but is there an analogous situation in moviegoing—a turn away from the present?

Advertisement

I am elated to report that this is not the case with moviegoing in New York City. On a recent Tuesday, for example, I went to a 1:00 PM showing at Film at Lincoln Center of Possible Love, the latest by the Korean director Lee Chang-dong. I had thought I might be one of a handful of people there, but I was one of about fifty. This is not an isolated incident. It seems that no matter when I see a new release—weekends or weekdays; morning, midday, or night—the spectators will always number, at the very least, in the double digits.

Not to belabor that comparison, but part of that argument was that novels used to be edited and shepherded through publication in a way they aren’t anymore. Of modern Hollywood’s many problems, is that one—that filmmakers or actors have less guidance than before?

If we’re talking specifically about Hollywood—that is, films backed by the major studios, or what’s left of them—then I’d argue that the problem is that there’s too much guidance, in that these movies have to follow a rigid template. Biopics that hit all of the same beats, for instance, or films—remakes, sequels, prequels—that exist solely as an extension of intellectual property. But in New York, this kind of cinema is a mere fraction of what’s available.

All American filmmakers, particularly those working independently, face the same struggle as their predecessors: getting funded. And yet every year excellent films by independent, US-based filmmakers that are true to their makers’ visions are released: in 2026 alone, that would include Steven Soderbergh’s The Christophers, John Early’s Maddie’s Secret, Lucio Castro’s Drunken Noodles, Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, among many others. I don’t wish to sound too sanguine. But since the medium began, bad or mediocre films have always outnumbered good or great ones.

Would you talk a bit about the critical approach you often take, of following actors through projects, rather than directors? It seems like the way so many more casual moviegoers decide what to watch but not many cinephiles, for some reason.

The fabulous term “acteurism” was coined by Dave Kehr, a longtime critic turned film curator, for a series he launched at MoMA in 2014 organized around the concept. He described the program as “devoted to actors who were able to develop their screen personalities with sufficient consistency and vivacity that they themselves became vehicles of meaning in their movies.” This was an especially helpful idea as I was writing a monograph on David Lynch’s Inland Empire, his final feature film and also his most labyrinthine. While never wishing to minimize Lynch, a director I revere, I thought it might be more fruitful to look at Laura Dern, Inland Empire’s star and a frequent Lynch collaborator, as the film’s coauthor. At the very least, what Dern does in this frequently confounding movie helps make it legible, lucid.

And although he never used the term, the incomparable gay cult film critic Boyd McDonald was also an acteurist partisan. In a review collected in his 1985 collection, Cruising the Movies, he waggishly writes, referring to the actor Richard Widmark, “He demonstrates the importance of the movie star over the movie and thus the importance of star reviews over mere movie reviews, with their constant complaints about plot.” Those words are never far from my mind whenever I’m writing about a film toward which I’m ambivalent but that boasts a performance that intrigues me, as was the case with Léa Seydoux in David Cronenberg’s Crimes of the Future from 2022.

Based on anecdotal evidence, younger cinephiles seem to have more of an acteurist bent. At recent tributes to actresses like Diane Keaton (at Walter Reade) and María Félix (at MoMA), for example, I was thrilled to be surrounded by so many movie lovers under the age of thirty-five in these high holy temples of cinema. As Barthes would have it in “The Face of Garbo”—perhaps the acteurist urtext—the visages of these performers “plunged [us] into the deepest ecstasy.”

entries.title: The Cost of Monetizing Everything
entries.summary: Behavioral economists prided themselves on bringing rational thinking to public policy, but behind their “nudges” for optimizing consumer behavior was a big corporate push.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
As we attempt to survive a government more given to punches than nudges, it is now possible to ask what remains of the decades-long project of applying behavioral economics to public policy. In the spring of 2008, a few weeks after the collapse of Bear Stearns but two months before Barack Obama secured the Democratic nomination, Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein published their book Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness. Thaler was one of the founders of the field of behavioral economics and went on to win the Nobel Prize in 2017. Sunstein was, and remains, probably the most prominent and influential legal scholar in the United States, and he is the author of dozens of books, four of them in 2024 alone. Nudge was a stampeding best seller, republished in a thoroughly revised version in 2021. In the meantime Sunstein, who had been a colleague and informal adviser of Obama’s at the University of Chicago Law School, served as the administrator of the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (sometimes known as the “regulatory czar”) from 2009 to 2012. He returned as senior counselor to the secretary of Homeland Security during the Biden administration.

Nudge set out the findings from decades of research in behavioral economics and the policy agenda that resulted. As Thaler recounts in his book Misbehaving (2015), which is a kind of memoir and tour through the history of the subject, behavioral economics began in the 1970s with the observation that most real people do not behave like the efficient, rational, calculating agents that economic theory presumes them to be. They make mistakes, they have cognitive and behavioral biases, they work from imperfect information, and they “miswant,” meaning they want things that they know are harmful, or at least they behave in ways that are inconsistent with their stated goals. Thaler set out to develop what he called “an enriched approach to doing economic research,” one that was “not a different discipline: it is still economics, but it is economics done with strong injections of good psychology and other social sciences…to improve the accuracy of the predictions made with [economic] theories.” He drew on research in behavioral psychology, especially the work of Daniel Kahneman, the author of the best-selling Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011) and himself a Nobel laureate in 2002.

By the early 2000s Thaler and his colleagues (including Sunstein) had developed a concept they called “libertarian paternalism.” They argued that there are many situations in which an individual or organization must make a choice that will shape or limit the choices of others, and since there is no such thing as a neutral choice, that makes some form of paternalism inevitable. Recognizing this means selecting policies that make affected parties better off by uncoercively shaping the “choice architecture” they face. As Thaler and Sunstein put it, “It is legitimate for choice architects to try to influence people’s behavior in order to make their lives longer, healthier, and better.”

The famous example that opens Nudge is a cafeteria line. We might believe that it is good for people to eat healthy food, and indeed that they want to eat healthy food, but sometimes they make mistakes and eat an entire pizza instead. So the cafeteria can put the healthy food at the front of the line where hungry people will likely take more of it instead of the less healthy options further along. The cafeteria has to put something first, and people are still choosing what to eat instead of being coerced, so the principles of libertarian paternalism are satisfied. Or, as Thaler put it, “Our premise was simple. Because people are Humans, not Econs…they make predictable errors. If we can anticipate those errors, we can devise policies that will reduce the error rate.”

Other examples proliferated. If we want people to save for retirement, opting in to saving should be the default, not opting out. If we want more organ donors, we should make people choose one way or another when they renew their driver’s licenses. If we want men to navigate urinals more competently, we should give them a target to aim at. These ideas set fire to the minds of policymakers around the world after the 2008 crisis. David Cameron established a Nudge Unit in the UK upon taking office in 2010, and by 2014 there were 136 countries that claimed to incorporate behavioral sciences into policymaking, fifty-one of them with centrally directed policy initiatives.

Reviewing Nudge in these pages, the journalist John Cassidy pointed out that the Obama administration’s economic philosophy wasn’t Keynesianism or Chicago-school libertarianism but behavioralism. Indeed, in September 2015 the administration issued Executive Order 13707 to “more fully realize the benefits of behavioral insights and deliver better results at a lower cost for the American people.” In retrospect, the nudge movement was emblematic of 2010s technocratic neoliberalism, combining an abiding faith in free markets as solutions to social problems with an antiseptic dislike of the real work of politics as well as an affinity for cleverness in policy design. Reading the books of its leading proponents now feels like the excavation of a lost world.

Advertisement

In their new book, It’s On You, Nick Chater and George Loewenstein come to bury the nudgers, not to praise them. Chater is a professor of behavioral science at Warwick Business School, and Loewenstein was a student of Thaler’s and is himself one of the central pillars of behavioral economics. Thaler describes him as one of the “leaders of the field” and the only one who “has really created much new psychology.” As a result, the book has undertones of apostasy and parricide. It is a critique from within, showing a wealth of insider knowledge and personal familiarity with behavioral economics and its practitioners.

In Chater and Loewenstein’s diagnosis, behavioral economists and their psychologist colleagues have been too “focused on the shortcomings of individuals” and have been busy “running experiments and documenting the many ‘imperfections’ of human judgment and decision-making.” This unreflective tendency to use the sovereign individual as the unit of analysis has meant that the entire field has been “misled into believing that individuals created these problems, and that individuals can fix them.”

Chater and Loewenstein call this way of thinking the “i-frame,” counterposed to the “s-frame” of systemic approaches to social problems. (That awkward nomenclature is one of the many ways this book still follows the genre conventions of pop behavioralism.) “Thinking in terms of the i-frame,” they write,

we take the rules of the game as fixed and ask how we can encourage or help the players to play the game better. Thinking in terms of the s-frame, we take human nature as fixed and ask how the rules of the game can be reshaped to produce better outcomes.

But really the book is not a methodological intervention or an argument for how to incorporate systemic approaches into behavioral models. It is a political economy critique. “Rather than i-frame policies arising organically by popular demand,” they write, “or out of policymakers’ natural inclinations, we found in case after case that there were corporate interests advancing i-frame solutions and perspectives.” In subject after subject and field after field, Chater and Loewenstein set out to show that the behavioral science experts have been at best the useful idiots of corporate interests or at worst their paid henchmen. As they put it:

While publicly advocating the i-frame, corporations spend substantial resources on lobbying, funding think tanks, and sponsoring academic research to ensure that the game is, and remains, rigged in their favor. This is the corporate sleight of hand: point to the i-frame act on the s-frame; rig the rules of the game, but blame individual citizens for any resulting social ills.

Chater and Loewenstein pursue this line of argument through chapters focused on several examples: climate change and the idea of carbon footprints, food and obesity, retirement saving, the American health care industry, and then in a kind of lightning-round chapter on plastic waste, privacy laws, prescription drug addiction, gun violence, and automobile deaths. In each case they show the same pattern: “attempts by industry to cast problems as the responsibility of individuals, coupled with lobbying to maintain the status quo.”

Their account of industry spending extends beyond lobbyists to policy practitioners and researchers. For example, “while academics who take positions supporting the food industry are well funded, those who criticize the industry are often undermined, either by the industry’s enlisting the support of other industry-aligned academics or by more direct means.” Or take the health care system, which is a nightmarish hellscape because the fee-for-service model creates “an almost unfathomable variety of conflicts of interest, arising from a vast array of deeply flawed incentives.” Again and again, they point to experts who claimed to be producing nuanced, sober behavioral science but who in fact were snarfling in the trough of corporate money and have then told a story (including to themselves and one another) about individual responsibility. In many cases, they probably didn’t even realize it. “The self-serving bias,” Chater and Loewenstein write, “kicks in when there are multiple interpretations of what is ‘fair.’ In such situations, people tend to choose whatever interpretation best suits their own interests.”

Worse still, it appears that the nudges didn’t even work. Chater and Loewenstein cite one meta-study of 241 nudge interventions that found a 1.4 percent change in the targeted behaviors; another survey of eighty-three randomized control trials on climate change nudges found at best a tiny effect during the course of the experiment and nothing afterward.

Further, the global nudge mania in the 2010s was not merely a frustrating mistake. The focus on the nudges crowded out other possibilities, both in research and in policy. Instead of trying to turn the Titanic, the nudgers were rearranging the order of the cafeteria line. More distressingly, they justified inaction on urgent, potentially catastrophic problems. “The green-energy nudge,” for example, “gives people the false hope that the problem of climate change can be addressed without imposing costlier, but immeasurably more effective, policies.”

Advertisement

Another perverse finding is that markets can offset any nudge-friendly individual action. Perhaps you choose not to fly, because of the environmental cost of air travel. Your contribution to reducing demand might then lower the cost of plane tickets, causing other people to fly more, thereby negating your individual decision. The point about the illusion of market choices can go even further. I can choose from a bewildering parade of health care plans, but I cannot choose universal health care that is free at the point of service. I can choose among different books to read, but it is difficult to buy one without enriching a tech oligarch. We can choose within market structures but not nonmarket forms of social relations. Most of us are not consulted in the decisions that structure our lives, leaving us with “choices” that are less and less meaningful.

Chater and Loewenstein are not subtle about whom and what to blame. They point to the neoliberal ideology of Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s, which constituted “a radical reshaping of the rules of society that systematically favored powerful businesses as well as the wealthy.” A chapter on inequality traces the rise of our current oligarchs and the ways their concentrated power has distorted incentives everywhere. In turn, people who really should know better but who are in some way complicit with big business or dependent on the spigot of oligarch money have collectively decided to blame the victims. Thus:

When a situation seems unfair, we first try to take actions to restore fairness. But if and when these actions fail, or when there is simply no action we can take, we try to reduce the painful sense of unfairness. And an effective way to do this is to find a way to rationalize that the victim of the injustice deserves the apparent injustice.

They don’t follow the thought further, but it has a clear political implication. Most people don’t much like being blamed by clever experts who aren’t actually helping. The present widespread distrust and outright loathing of expertise in health, economics, education, and academia might well be partly attributable to this habit. Or it could be the other way around: deservedness is such a core principle of American public discourse that sincere policy wonks can’t perceive that they are reproducing the problems they are trying to solve. The i-frame is so deeply ingrained that it shapes even efforts at s-frame thinking. Either way, the dispensation of class power continues unabated.

Cass Sunstein’s latest book, The Price of Happiness, is a defense of “willingness to pay” (which he abbreviates WTP), a concept that is at the heart of determining which policy or regulation is “best” and thus which should be preferred from a behavioral science perspective. Willingness to pay means assigning prices to things like sunsets, the last blue whale, or the lives of your children in order to assess tradeoffs and relative preferences. How much more would you want to be paid to do a dangerous job? How much would you be willing to pay your neighbor to be quiet? How much would your neighbor be willing to pay you to keep ventilating their nocturnal music? One central price is the value of a single statistical life, which at the time of this writing is $14.1 million, although the Trump administration is trying very hard to drive it to zero.*

This is far from the first work on the subject: Richard Thaler’s first academic paper, published in 1976, was titled “The Value of Saving a Life.” This is not even Cass Sunstein’s first book on it: at the very least, his Risk and Reason (2002), Valuing Life (2014), and The Cost-Benefit Revolution (2018) each build a similar case. The concept of willingness to pay was first developed by Alfred Marshall in 1890, and most of the theoretical elaborations and limitations were figured out between the “externalities” of A.C. Pigou in the 1910s and the libertarian Ronald Coase’s answer in 1960 that assigning property rights to everything would solve social problems. A 1989 law review article announced “Willingness to Pay Comes of Age.” By 2026 it must be approaching retirement. Why this book, and why now?

The Price of Happiness is intended to be a discussion of the objections to the willingness to pay model and a vindication of its usefulness. People might misprice things because of the range of behavioral biases familiar to behavioral economists: they are unreasonably optimistic, they have self-control problems, they have short time horizons and limited attention, or they dislike losses more than they like gains. They may not have enough information. “An uninformed choice is not exactly autonomous,” Sunstein writes. “A choice produced by present bias or limited attention is not fully autonomous.” These conditions raise problems for the applicability and accuracy of making regulatory, legal, or economic decisions based on what people say they are willing to pay for something, and that in turn leaves extensive precincts of human life where this approach is inappropriate. “If a low WTP shows a failure to give adequate attention to the future,” he writes, by way of example, “then there is reason not to use WTP.”

Sunstein discusses many other limitations. Some things, like true love or the right to be racist, cannot or should not be bought and sold in markets. Some pricing choices affect other people who are not consulted, which he calls “a real problem…. A great deal of work remains to be done on this topic.” He acknowledges that some things, like justice and deliberative democracy, are probably best approached by treating people as citizens, not consumers. He is aware that rich people have more money than poor people, but also that money has a diminishing marginal utility such that the same amount means less to a rich person than to a poor person. “Here, then, is a problem for WTP. A poor person might be willing to pay much less than [Elon] Musk for some good, even though Musk would benefit much less than the poor person from that good.” And so on.

But Sunstein does have a political point to advance. As he puts it:

No one, rich or poor, should be forced to pay more than she is willing to pay for goods, including the reduction of risks. In fact this idea embodies a norm of equality (and the right one). If poor people are unwilling to pay much for the reduction of serious risks, and if government wants to help, the appropriate response is not a compelled purchase but a subsidy, perhaps in the form of cash payments.

He concludes that despite its limitations, willingness to pay is “usually a pretty good measure of the likely welfare effects of obtaining goods” and “is a way of respecting people’s autonomy.” So, in the end, “choice, freedom, and WTP are linked.”

The cumulative effect is like watching Sunstein tear down his house in order to build a fence. The objections are so numerous and varied, the acceptable scope for the willingness to pay model becomes so circumscribed, and Sunstein spends so little time solving each problem that the book is almost self-refuting. Rather than persuasive rebuttals or preponderant evidence, his case depends on his characteristic argumentative style.

In The Price of Happiness and elsewhere, Sunstein pursues his argument along three lines. The first is practical: nudges (or willingness to pay, or cost-benefit analysis) are effective, as shown by behavioral science, and a good tool for measurement or other technical tasks. The second is institutional: nudges (et al.) are the best way to accomplish what the legal system is trying to do. And the third is philosophical: nudges are tangible expressions of utilitarian philosophy, which Sunstein takes as the best moral system. He often quotes the work of John Stuart Mill, but the more humane parts of Mills’s oeuvre (of which there are many, to be sure) and not the parts advocating “benevolent despotism” in the colonies or explaining that liberty is not for “those backward states of society in which the race itself may be considered as in its nonage.”

Sunstein’s characteristic procedure is to slide between these three levels of argument as needed. The objection that nudges don’t work in practice is met by an appeal to utilitarian philosophy; objections to utilitarianism itself are answered by saying that nudges are the best we can do with the legal system we have. Objections to the legal system are diverted to questions about efficacy or morality.

When I read Sunstein, I am seldom persuaded by him, but it’s never because I can think of something he hasn’t. He knows the criticisms of utilitarianism perfectly well, he is aware of the inequities of the American legal system, and he admits there are many arenas where his approaches don’t actually work, but he can’t or won’t put all three of those problems together. Similarly, Sunstein is well aware of the many critiques of nudges. He responded to them at length in Why Nudge? (2014) and The Ethics of Influence (2016). The 2021 reissue of Nudge features a chapter of responses to critics. He doesn’t find them persuasive, but his reasons are not always clear. Sometimes he seems to believe there are no alternatives, but neither does he look for any. The certainty and volume of his output is impressive, but it’s easy to wonder about the marginal utility of one more of these books.

It’s On You is in some ways a powerful and coruscating book; in other ways, it is very frustrating. The evidentiary chapters are clear and lively. They also explain critiques of structural inequalities that have been made by a legion of sociologists, historians, journalists, activists, and many others for decades. Chater and Loewenstein say their eyes were opened by reading Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway’s The Big Myth (2023), about the twentieth-century corporate propaganda campaign for free market fundamentalism that involved everything from Reagan’s acting career to the Little House on the Prairie books. The Big Myth is an effective text, but there is something dispiriting about two “libertarian paternalists” discovering in the year 2023 why the political left exists.

This delayed revelation itself seems symptomatic. As the historian Daniel Rodgers showed in Age of Fracture (2011), since about the 1970s American intellectual, civic, and political life has been pulverized by the market, transforming communities into collections of atomized, alienated individuals. That condition of market-dependent isolation was mistaken for human nature, and the attendant collapse of social and associational life made it difficult for many people to conceive of collective action as an academic subject or a political project. No wonder behavioral economists and policymakers couldn’t see systems: they inhabited a world of consuming individuals, not a world of social meaning and communal belonging; they took that condition as a given, not as the outcome of politics.

It is not necessary to agree with all of Chater and Loewenstein’s story to be convinced that the behavioralists committed a profound category error. As Thaler explains in Misbehaving, the point of behavioral economics was to improve the accuracy and realism of economic modeling. That is an estimable goal, but it is not a political philosophy or a principle of governance, let alone a method for delivering happy lives. Thaler goes on to claim that “designing good public policies has a lot in common with designing any consumer product,” and therein lies the problem. Looking at public policy through goggles designed to explain consumer choice has turned out to be perfectly consistent with a free-market reductionist view of the world, so instead of pushing back against Chicago-school libertarianism, the behavioralists strengthened it and inoculated it against criticism.

They found an ideological home in a Democratic Party that had developed a fastidious distaste for politics itself, mistaking what is actually a ruthless zero-sum power struggle for a well-meaning bipartisan effort to solve technical problems while leaving the shape of inequality undisturbed. They substituted an antipolitics for the creation of a positive vision of society at exactly the moment when something new was necessary, a move that constituted a unilateral disarmament in the face of an intransigent radical right wing. A pivotal decade or more was lost in which no meaningful action was taken against climate change or inequality, but a lot of calorie counts got displayed.

That category slippage is evident in the final chapters of It’s On You. Having presented the insidious distortions of corporate power across a range of pressing social issues, Chater and Loewenstein end the book by offering suggestions not for how to rebalance the scales but for how to improve the methods of behavioral science. They wave toward the need for “exposing and breaking up these networks of influence” and say that solutions “will mean taking money out of politics across the board,” but most of their attention is turned to things like broadening graduate student training and better publication standards in academic journals. The unescapable implication is that their tools have left them unable to address the problems they’ve identified. They can see the s-frame now, but they don’t know what to do with it.

From the vantage point of 2026, the behavioralist approach is utterly incommensurable with the times. After DOGE, after the overturning of the Chevron doctrine and the Voting Rights Act, as a masked right-wing paramilitary shoots Americans in the streets and Donald Trump bombs other countries with impunity, the prospect that the government might be doing more regulation than poor people want does not seem especially urgent. While the Democrats were busy nudging, the Republicans took over the Supreme Court, gerrymandered the legislature, and gutted the administrative state. A mass politics to democratize the United States is not going to be based on nudges.

The empty political content of behavioral science, like that of these books, presupposes that most serious problems have already been solved or have only one consensus solution. In Nudge, The Price of Happiness, and elsewhere, Sunstein and his coauthors often write in the plural, about what “we” want: if “we” want to monetize things, or if “we” care about inequality, or if “we” want to anticipate people’s errors, then behavioral economics is the right method. But that presumes a political agent, someone who knows what people want and wants them to get it.

The tools can be turned to other uses. After all, strategically rearranging the presentation of products is well known to advertisers, marketers, and shopkeepers. Deciding to arrange the cafeteria line either to help diners lose weight or to help the cafeteria sell more food is a political choice that is elided in the behavioralist accounts. That elision, in turn, means the behavioralists seem not to have applied their ideas to themselves. Perhaps wanting to monetize everything is itself a form of miswanting, and the social cost of living in a world where everything has a price is higher than they realized. If the nudgers were nudged, then what matters is not the choice architecture presented to our human capital, but the decisions of actual capital.

entries.title: Arthur Schomburg’s Legacy
entries.summary: The Schomburg Center in Harlem is marking its centennial by celebrating the man whose library grew into one of the world’s great collections of black history and literature.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Arturo (Arthur) Schomburg was born in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in 1874. His mother was a black laundress from the Virgin Islands and his father a mestizo merchant of German descent long resident on the island. He came to New York in 1891 and joined the Cuban and Puerto Rican revolutionary movement, but factional disputes at the close of the Spanish-American War led him to turn his attention to the cause of black American freedom instead.

Schomburg was not just a “race man,” as activists used to be called, he was also an organization man. He belonged to a number of groups of pioneering black intellectuals. In 1911 he cofounded the Negro Society for Historical Research. In 1920 he was elected president of the American Negro Academy, of which W.E.B. Du Bois had been one of the original members when it was founded in Washington, D.C., in 1897. Alfred A. Moss Jr. in The American Negro Academy: Voice of the Talented Tenth (1981) observes that although Schomburg had written articles and had a reputation as a book collector, he did not have a college degree, and his election over more distinguished members was a sign to some of the Academy’s decline. Washington as the center of black intellectual life had been superseded by New York, and according to Moss, Schomburg was unable to attend to the Academy’s business in person. He was its last president when it folded in 1928.

The Harlem branch of the New York Public Library opened in 1905 on the corner of 135th Street and Lenox Avenue. By 1920, when the area was becoming overwhelmingly black, Ernestine Rose, the head librarian, and Catherine Latimer, the first black librarian there, believed that the branch needed a special reference collection to preserve the historical record of black people. Schomburg, a longtime patron of the library, was chairman of the committee that developed the plan for the Department of Negro Literature and History, which was established in 1925. The following year the Board of Trustees of the New York Public Library received a grant from the Carnegie Corporation to purchase his collection of 3,338 bound volumes. He was not paid what it was worth, Elinor Des Verney Sinnette tells us in Arthur Alfonso Schomburg: Black Bibliophile and Collector (1989), but he didn’t care too much. He knew what he had done. He served as curator of the collection from 1932 until his death in 1938, and the library was renamed the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture in 1972.

Because of the eventual fame of the collection, many people assumed that Schomburg was a philanthropist, but he’d amassed his library on a modest income. He searched in the warehouses and secondhand bookstores of New York at a time when what he was looking for was not of much value to most people. As a Caribbean-born Spanish speaker, he urged black Americans to look into black history before slavery and black culture in other countries, not just in the United States. He also took an interest in black artists, and in the early twentieth century he began making a collection of prints and etchings.

The Schomburg Center has been celebrating what its director, Joy L. Bivins, announced was a double centennial: that of the founding of the Department of Negro Literature and History as well as that of the Schomburg purchase. It has been marked by a year of events, starting last June with the launch of Joy Goddess: A’Lelia Walker and the Harlem Renaissance, a biography of the Jazz Age hostess and patron of the Dark Tower cultural salon by her great-granddaughter A’Lelia Bundles. Deborah Willis, an artist and former curator of photographs and prints at the Schomburg, interviewed Bundles on the Schomburg stage, and the line afterward for book signings and advice from Bundles on researching family stories extended out the lobby doors.

There have been evenings of music and film as well. The Schomburg Collection holds some five thousand motion pictures and videotapes. In May the series “Black on Screen: Inner Lives, Outer Frames” included the short film Cleopatra at the Mall (2024) by Madeleine Hunt-Ehrlich. It commemorates the rediscovery of The Death of Cleopatra, a large marble sculpture of the enthroned queen in death by the African American/Ojibwe artist Edmonia Lewis, which was exhibited in Philadelphia in 1876 and Chicago in 1878 and then forgotten until it was tracked down in storage at a Chicago mall by the art historian Marilyn Richardson in 1989.

The series also screened Losing Ground by Kathleen Collins, followed by a panel headed by Melissa Lyde, the founder of Alfreda’s Cinema in Brooklyn. The film follows a philosophy professor and her artist husband through a summer during which her ambitions and his wildness threaten the stability of their marriage. Made in 1982, Losing Ground had no commercial release. It is remembered not only as one of the first features directed by a black American woman but also as depicting a character seldom seen in American cinema: the intellectual black woman. Collins died at forty-six in 1988. A collection of her short stories, Whatever Happened to Interracial Love, was published posthumously in 2016 with a foreword by the poet and scholar Elizabeth Alexander.

The centennial celebrations continue with the exhibition “To Uncover and Reveal to the World: Arturo Schomburg’s Library.” It beautifully displays fifty-nine books and pamphlets from what the center’s former director Kevin Young called Schomburg’s “seed library”—the books he had collected and then donated to the Department of Negro Literature and History—as well as artworks and postcards related to his collecting activities. The exhibition expands our understanding of his contribution to the study of people of African descent. Handwritten minutes from Las Dos Antillas, the political club that the journalist Rafael Serra cofounded in 1892 to work for Cuban and Puerto Rican independence, remind us of Schomburg’s early activism in New York, when he served as the club’s secretary. Vanessa K. Valdés in Diasporic Blackness: The Life and Times of Arturo Alfonso Schomburg (2017) tells us that his outlook was always international, which sometimes put him at odds with those who preferred to concentrate on the black struggle in the US.

Some 160 languages are represented in the center’s collection. Poetas de Color (1887), for instance, a volume about Afro-Cuban poets edited by Francisco Calcagno, reflects Schomburg’s understanding of writing by black people as the literature of a diaspora. In addition to texts critical of Spanish colonialism, such as The Color Question in the Two Americas (1922) by Bernardo Ruiz Suarez, the exhibition features collections of Haitian records from 1741 to 1804 and works of Haitian history. Schomburg regarded Baron de Vastey, King Henri Christophe’s secretary, as an important thinker on questions of colonialism and race. Schomburg’s seed library includes Vastey’s Le Cri de la patrie (1815), a pamphlet whose title he translated as Cry of the Fatherland in the Interest of All Haytians. Among the other volumes on display concerned with the diaspora are From West Africa to Palestine (1873) by Edward Wilmot Blyden, often called the father of Pan-Africanism, and The African Abroad: or, His Evolution in Western Civilization (1913) by William H. Ferris, a Congregational pastor whose work introduced many black students to the ideas of Marcus Garvey.

David Bryant Fulton, a member of the Negro Society for Historical Research, published in 1900, under the pseudonym Jack Thorne, Hanover: or, The Persecution of the Lowly, his fictional account of the Wilmington, North Carolina, massacre in 1898, when white supremacists overthrew the Reconstruction municipal government, burned the black press, killed more than two dozen black people, and drove hundreds more from the city. Schomburg’s generously inscribed copy of Hanover is on display in the exhibition. The massacre is also the subject of Charles Chesnutt’s novel The Marrow of Tradition (1901), which is diplomatic about how complicit white business leaders and politicians were in the massacre compared to Fulton’s assertion that they financially underwrote the mobs. Chesnutt’s son-in-law, Edward Christopher Williams, the librarian of Howard University and the author of a witty epistolary novel about the black upper-middle class, When Washington Was in Vogue, which remained unpublished until 2004, had been elected a member of the American Negro Academy in 1911 during a period of optimism about its appeal to a new generation and the number of occasional papers it would publish. (Chesnutt, on the other hand, declined to become a member when the Academy was founded.)

The activists, educators, churchmen, editors, librarians, and writers involved in such institutions also formed the circle of bibliophiles with whom Schomburg could share his passion: Reverend Charles D. Martin, the founder of the Fourth Moravian Church in Harlem; William C. Bolivar, a collector in Philadelphia with a noteworthy library of books, pamphlets, tracts, manuscripts, and letters; John W. Cromwell, a lawyer, teacher, and author of The Negro in American History (1914); John Edward Bruce, a newspaper editor and columnist; George Washington Forbes, the first black librarian at the Boston Public Library; and George Young, whose Book Exchange in Harlem and catalog were important resources. Bruce was a cofounder with Schomburg of the Negro Society for Historical Research in 1911 and the Theban Literary Circle in 1921. They and their corresponding members on three continents collected works of black history in different languages. In Schomburg’s best-known essay, “The Negro Digs Up His Past,” published in Alain Locke’s The New Negro (1925), he was adamant that there was a “definite desire and determination to have a history, well documented, widely known at least within race circles, and administered as a stimulating and inspiring tradition for coming generations.”

John Edward Bruce, born into slavery, helped Schomburg rescue and have bound the handwritten manuscript of The Greatness of Christ and Other Sermons by Alexander Crummell (one of 240 manuscripts of historical importance in the Schomburg’s Manuscripts, Archives, and Rare Books Division). Crummell, the son of free black abolitionists in New York, was the first black graduate of Cambridge University, the founder of St. Luke’s Episcopal Church in Washington, D.C., and a cofounder of the American Negro Academy, and he was remembered by Du Bois in The Souls of Black Folk as one of the inspirations of his youth. Bruce, who died in 1924, was a freemason like Schomburg, a stalwart supporter of Garvey, and the great-uncle of the Harlem Renaissance gay bohemian artist and writer Richard Bruce Nugent.
