The exhibition’s informative companion volume of essays, Black Studies on 135th Street: The Founding and Future of the Schomburg Collection, edited by Barrye Brown, Laura E. Helton, and Vanessa K. Valdés, says that the number of books in Schomburg’s library was known, but no detailed inventory survived. Curators painstakingly searched books for clues such as his bookplates, inscriptions, and address stamps. Nearly a third of the book is a fascinating bibliography, edited by Helton and compiled with the help of Schomburg Center staff, of Schomburg’s seed library.

Some of the collection’s holdings were known to have been his because they meant so much to him. For instance, the first comprehensive survey of writings by people of African descent was published in France in 1808: the Abbé Henri Grégoire’s De la littérature des Nègres: ou, Recherches sur leurs facultés intellectuelles, leurs qualités morales et leur littérature; suivies de notices sur la vie et les ouvrages des nègres qui se sont distingués dans les sciences, les lettres et les arts. Grégoire belonged to the school of Enlightenment writers who campaigned to refute the notion that black people were inferior to white people. He rushed to have the book translated into English because the Napoleonic state was in turmoil and he expected the French edition to be suppressed at any moment. It was published in Brooklyn in 1810 under the title An Enquiry Concerning the Intellectual and Moral Faculties, and Literature of Negroes; Followed with an account of the Life and Works of Fifteen Negroes and Mulattoes, Distinguished in Science, Literature and the Arts. Schomburg later had other sources of writings by black people, such as Henri Ternaux-Compans’s Catalogue des livres et manuscrits de la bibliothèque de feu M. Raetzal (1836), but Grégoire’s book was his first guide and inspiration.

Among the other books on display in the exhibition is a 1550 translation of De partibus divinae legis libri duo doctissimi, omnibus theologiae studiosis apprime vtiles…, the exploration of divine law by the sixth-century North African bishop Junillus Africanus; a 1632 edition of Leo Africanus’s Description of Africa; and The Travels of the Jesuits in Ethiopia, a translation of the writings of Manuel da Almeida, a seventeenth-century Portuguese Jesuit ambassador to Ethiopia, published anonymously in 1710, half a century after Almeida’s death. Jacobus Elisa Joannes Capitein, born in 1717 in what is now Ghana, was enslaved at an early age, but in keeping with certain social experiments of the Enlightenment, he studied as a free man at the University of Leiden. Political Research Paper on Slavery is a translation of his 1742 dissertation, Staatkundig-godgeleerd onderzoekschrift over de slaverny…, for his degree in theology. Capitein argued that support of slavery favored the propagation of the Gospel and he returned to Ghana in 1742 as a missionary, where he died.

Schomburg was so taken with Phillis Wheatley and her Poems on Various Occasions, Religious and Moral (1773), the first book by a black person to be published in English, that he also began collecting books she had owned, such as The Works in Verse and Prose of William Shenstone (1773). In her essay in Black Studies on 135th Street, Tara A. Bynum tells us that Schomburg’s reverence for Wheatley led him to purchase every edition of her poems and letters that he could find. The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or: Gustavus Vassa, the African, Written by Himself was published in London in 1789. Equiano’s autobiography was celebrated by Grégoire as the first slave narrative written without editorial direction or intervention from a white person. He compares Equiano’s style to that of Defoe and marvels at his power to convey what it was like to see white people, a ship, the ocean, flying fish, snow, and a watch for the first time. Schomburg owned copies of the English and American first editions of Equiano’s book as well as five early-nineteenth-century reprints.

The exhibition includes Religious Experience and Journal of Mrs. Jarena Lee, Giving an Account of Her Call to Preach the Gospel (1849), a defiant work, considering that women were not wanted as preachers. The copies of Eric Walrond’s Tropic Death (1926) and Claude McKay’s Home to Harlem (1922) have very personal inscriptions to Schomburg. They say as much as the accompanying newspaper articles by Walrond and Zora Neale Hurston about how important Schomburg was to the Harlem Renaissance writers. Black Studies on 135th Street reminds us that when McKay was abroad, he depended on Schomburg for help with research and money. Schomburg’s seed library includes Langston Hughes’s first book, The Weary Blues, and Steven G. Fullwood, a former assistant curator in the Manuscript, Archives, and Rare Books Division, tells us in his contribution that Schomburg didn’t just collect Hughes’s work; Hughes sent him books he found on his travels and continued to send books to the collection after Schomburg’s death.

In 1972 the director William Greaves gathered several witnesses to and participants in the Harlem Renaissance at the apartment of Duke Ellington—among them Eubie Blake, Leigh Whipper, Aaron Douglas, Richard Bruce Nugent, Arna Bontemps, George Schuyler, Romare Bearden, and Richard B. Moore—to remember those days and to discuss the impact of the period. Greaves’s son, David Greaves, sifted through 60,000 feet of the film his father shot that afternoon and assembled the selections into the recently released Once Upon a Time in Harlem, a warm and moving documentary. At one point in it, Regina Anderson Andrews, hired as a librarian at the 135th Street branch library in 1923, remembers how the young writers and poets of the Harlem Renaissance would come to sit and write, to feel at home and protected in the quiet.

Schomburg used the money from the sale of his library in 1926 to go on a hunt for books in Europe. He had given an address to the Negro Academy in 1923 on the subject of Juan de Pareja, the painter enslaved to Velázquez. In 1926 Schomburg had the director of the Prado in Madrid unlock several doors to reveal Pareja’s Calling of Saint Matthew (1661), which portrays the well-dressed painter as the sole figure in the composition looking directly at the viewer, though he is on the edge of the painting. Antonio Palomino in his history of eminent Spanish painters tells the story of Velázquez painting Pareja in Rome in 1650 and then having him deliver himself the portrait intended for exhibition at the Pantheon. Those who saw the painted canvas, so dignified and alive, stared in amazement at it and then at Pareja, not knowing which to address or which would answer them.

The Metropolitan Museum invited the Schomburg Center to be a part of its exhibition “Juan de Pareja, Afro-Hispanic Painter” in 2023, because Schomburg had been the first to attempt a catalogue raisonné of his work and because he had been the only one to write about Pareja in the early twentieth century. The exhibition displayed some of the works from the sixteenth century that had been in Schomburg’s seed library as well as a work he purchased in 1932 and cherished: Ad catholicum pariter et invictissimum Phillippum Dei gratia Hispaniarum regem by Juan Latino, the Ethiopian-born, emancipated Latinist at the University of Granada, of which only two copies survive. A collection of poems and epigrams, it was printed in Granada in 1573 in tribute to Don Juan of Austria, the illegitimate son of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, who led the fleet that defeated the Ottomans at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571, and in praise of Philip II of Spain.

The gallery for the Schomburg exhibition is designed to evoke the wallpaper and hearth of his parlor. Schomburg’s family—he had eight children—put up with the ever-increasing number of books. They understood. Also on display are photographs of his modest homes, first in Harlem, then Brooklyn. The postcards of the nineteenth-century black actor Ira Aldridge and images of Wheatley and Dumas remind us that the collection first had a domestic setting. There are several works by Albert Alexander Smith, a black artist who lived in Paris in the 1920s and 1930s: watercolors of Wheatley and Rene Maran, the author of Batouala (1921), the Goncourt Prize–winning novel that offered the first positive portrait of primitivism; and portraits of Dumas and Pushkin.

William Ward’s mezzotint of the Chevalier de Saint-Georges, the eighteenth-century composer from Guadeloupe, hangs high on a gallery wall, and it is his opera, L’Amant anonyme, that we are hearing as we look at Schomburg’s books. One of Saint-Georges’s concertantes is among the audio selections available on a “Listening Wall” in the Schomburg lobby, which range from Yoruba dundun drums and Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s “Hiawatha’s Wedding Feast” to a 1925 recording of Paul Robeson intoning “Water Boy,” and a 1960 recording of Harry Belafonte singing “Steal Away.”

The Schomburg’s collection of books and rare manuscripts, music and oral history recordings, prints and photographs amount to more than 11,000,000 items. And yet this is a very intimate exhibition, a moving portrait of a cultural hero. For book lovers, it is a dream. It is also affirming. The Schomburg Center is not a locked-up campus or a school library under threat of books that have been deemed dangerous to the young being removed by a local authority. It is full of what had been commercial failures and what had been unwanted, offensive, opposed. Its collection challenges the well-meaning tendency in US publishing to internalize the will to censorship. That the Jazz Age is one hundred years ago feels weird. But the liberations set in motion since World War I go on, right along with the urge to defeat them. A power-stupid administration may be seeking to impose revisions of history on a nation’s educational institutions and museums, but as A’Lelia Bundles has said, nothing can stop us from telling our stories.

I remember being in a penitential mood on my first visit to the Schomburg. It was 1981 and the Schomburg’s new building, the work of J. Max Bond Jr., had opened a few months before. I’d never been in the old building, by McKim, Mead, and White, and when introduced elsewhere to its curator of many years, Jean Blackwell Hutson, I was ignorant of her importance.

In the lobby there was a portrait of Schomburg and a bronze and white marble bust of Ira Aldridge, dressed for his most famous role, Othello, by the Milanese sculptor Pietro Calvi, who supplied polychrome marble busts of black people for the smoking rooms of Europe in the days when white gentlemen wanted such sentries as evidence they’d traveled. Stairs took me down to the reading room and to a room of machines where I could squint at the microfilm of the beautiful handwriting of Paul Laurence Dunbar’s desperate letters to his absconded wife, Alice. Dunbar disliked Whitman.

A bust of Miss Hutson presided over the card catalog, the rows of little drawers like shelves in an ossuary. In the Jean Blackwell Hutson Research and Reference Division, among lithographs by Jacob Lawrence and Paul Colin, the Romare Bearden collage, busts by Richmond Barthé, Bo Walker’s wood sculpture of Frederick Douglass, the Norman Lewis, Archibald Motley, and Malvin Gray Johnson paintings, the library staff was coping with the afternoon’s crop of whispering students, scholars, sons constructing family trees, and a loud crazy who had mysterious reasons for not wanting to check her wrinkled plastic bags in the cloakroom upstairs. I was another. In the downstairs reading room, with the sunken courtyard of birch and ivy, under the murals by Aaron Douglas, under something that resembled an electronic bingo board that told you when the books you had asked for had come from the stacks, I sat down.

entries.title: We Tell Ourselves Stories in Order to Change
entries.summary: In the films and fiction of Jane Schoenbrun, the boundary between reality and fantasy is porous, alluring, and must be carefully patrolled.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
“There is a hole at the bottom of the lake where the movies come from,” the reclusive former scream queen Billy Presley announces in Jane Schoenbrun’s newest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Maybe so—Schoenbrun’s astonishing creative output over the past several years certainly suggests some such occult source. In addition to three feature films—We’re All Going to the World’s Fair (2021), I Saw the TV Glow (2024), and Teenage Sex—Schoenbrun has now written a nearly six-hundred-page novel, Public Access Afterworld. Individually, each work is, to varying degrees, a success. Taken together, they form the kind of ambitious, labyrinthine corpus that most artists require a lifetime to create.*

Schoenbrun’s three features, sometimes referred to as the “screen trilogy,” all involve strikingly similar characters and plot elements that are revisited to wildly different tonal effect: a depressed, dark-haired young woman with a subdued demeanor and wide, shattered eyes disappears into a fantasy world of uncertain epistemic status, closely observed by a masculine figure whose motivations are difficult to parse.

In We’re All Going to the World’s Fair, the young woman is a teenage girl named Casey, and the world is a collaborative online horror “challenge,” an ostensibly occult ritual played out via shared YouTube videos and Skype calls. Casey, who lives alone with her father, catches the attention of JLB, an adult man who participates in the game. (In 2018 Schoenbrun made a documentary, A Self-Induced Hallucination, consisting entirely of stitched-together clips from YouTube inspired by the horror phenomenon Slender Man, and World’s Fair demonstrates a correspondingly intimate knowledge of the messy DIY landscape of online horror, as well as the quirky, creative, youthful community that gave rise to it.) Structured and marketed as a horror movie, as all of Schoenbrun’s films have been, World’s Fair is the one that comes closest to actually meeting the demands of the genre: a clean setup, building tension, gross-out moments, the occasional jump scare. Yet the primary emotion the film evokes is not fear but the crushing loneliness, akin to grief, that is the hallmark of emotional neglect.

In I Saw the TV Glow, meanwhile, the young woman is Maddy, and the fantasy world is a TV show she loves called The Pink Opaque. Her observer is a teenage schoolmate named Owen, and his motives are less ominous than JLB’s but in some ways equally, well, opaque—he desires Maddy’s friendship, but with the yearning, painful intensity of a teenage crush. Their relationship is complicated by the fact that Maddy is queer, while Owen does not understand—or cannot accept—himself as trans. Via the fantasy world of The Pink Opaque, Maddy and Owen can relate to each other as two women, with a shared, straightforward destiny; in the real world, that’s too painful for Owen to contemplate. He tells Maddy, “When I think about that stuff [i.e., sex] it feels like someone took a shovel and dug out all my insides, and I know there’s nothing in there, but I’m still too nervous to open myself up and check.”

The same month The Pink Opaque is canceled, Maddy runs away, and Owen is too frightened to follow her. Maddy returns, years later, to make an astonishing claim: The Pink Opaque is real, and it’s this world—the world of the suburbs, of jobs and family and grinding sameness—that is the illusion. She entreats Owen to follow her into The Pink Opaque, but again he refuses, caught by both his fear and his allegiance to the people he’d be forced to abandon. He is left only with a crushing despair and fantasies of what could have been:

What if she was right?… What if I really was someone else? Someone beautiful and powerful? Someone buried alive and suffocating to death, very far away, on the other side of a television screen?

The most straightforward reading of the movie is one in which The Pink Opaque stands in for the possibility of authenticity: transition, queerness, heroism, and art as the true reality, counterposed with the stifling lie of the conventional, closeted life. Both World’s Fair and TV Glow, though studded with flashes of beauty and wit, are on the whole emotionally punishing—even devastating—films. They mimic the slippery, dissociative fugue states in which their protagonists are trapped: all the characters are deeply isolated and, despite their best efforts at connection, can’t help talking past one another. The rules always seem to be shifting, the passage of time feels muddy and irrational, and it’s hard to tell what’s real.

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, Schoenbrun’s most recent film, at first seems to break that mold. The main characters are two women: Gillian Anderson’s Billy Presley and Hannah Einbinder’s Kris Williams, an up-and-coming queer filmmaker who visits Billy at her remote movie-set-turned-country-house. The film is joyful, warm, funny, extremely sexy, and endlessly self-referential: a horror fan’s delight, minus any actual scares. Watching it, one is tempted to imagine Kris’s life as the one Maddy might have had after she escaped from the suburbs. No longer isolated or punished for her queerness, she is instead celebrated for it. Despite having made only one tiny art house film (a remake of Psycho “from the perspective of the shower curtain”), she’s been hired to reboot the “zombie IP” of the once popular, now problematic Camp Miasma slasher franchise—that is, to make it acceptably woke. She has an open relationship with her girlfriend, who is, in turn, dating a bisexual man named Thor. Her mission is straightforward, and her enemies (sexism, racism, transphobia) clearly identifiable. The only problem is…none of it feels quite real.

Advertisement

Enter, once again, a dark-haired young woman with wide, shattered eyes. This time she is the character played by a young Billy Presley (Amanda Fix), the protagonist of the first Camp Miasma film, who is stalked and murdered by its recurring villain, Little Death. Little Death is the ghost of a child who was bullied and then drowned by other campers because of his ambiguous gender, and the bond between him and Billy is heightened, and made strange, by the fact that though Little Death murders her, her experience of the encounter is one of erotic fulfillment: “little death” (la petite mort) is a euphemism for “orgasm,” and Billy has her first one while imagining herself through the eyes of Little Death as he kills her character. The wide-eyed girl and the one who obsessively watches her: there they are again, that mysterious pair.

Toward the end of the film, on a call with a bunch of soulless movie execs, Kris tries to explain what she’s discovered from Billy, the truth of Camp Miasma: that though the filmmakers thought they invented Little Death, in fact Little Death is the one who created them. “You all are characters in a movie!” she cries. “We are a movie for him to edit, and he has final cut.” It’s the same message that Maddy fought her way back to Owen to deliver: your understanding of the world is upside down; your reality is fantasy; the fantasy is realer than real.

At the climax (ha) of the movie, after Kris moves through a dreamlike scenario in which Little Death slaughters all the people who irritated her, the adult Billy gently but firmly coaxes Kris through a sexual encounter in which Kris lets go of her hang-ups and allows herself to experience the desire underneath the shame. Then Little Death turns his murderous gaze (and weapon) on Billy and Kris. The film suggests that feelings that begin in trauma—whether discomfort with the body you were born in or an imagined identification with the person who has harmed you—can be revisited and reclaimed in fantasy. This discovery, though frightening at first, ultimately allows Billy and Kris the freedom to slip back and forth between worlds at will, playfully weaving fantasy and reality together in a way that brings them genuine happiness.

For all the blood and guts and screaming, Teenage Sex is an exuberant, life-affirming film, a joyful celebration of queer sexuality and a sharp-eyed but loving tribute to the imperfect cultural ephemera that have helped shape it. Beneath the pop sensibility, there is a serious argument about the primacy of desire, the way it bursts through logical, moral, and aesthetic barriers. The body pushes beyond what the mind considers acceptable, overwhelming and dissolving the thinking self, and bringing with it a capacity for renewal, generation, and rebirth. Desire always comes first; the intellect trails behind it like a shadow. And only when the mind surrenders to the body, and the critic to the artist, can satisfaction be achieved—and new art be born.

The trilogy, it seems, has a happy ending. But then here comes Public Access Afterworld, throwing everything into confusion, like Jason surfacing to drag the final girl underwater right before the credits roll in Friday the 13th.

Public Access Afterworld is closer in tone to Teenage Sex than to Schoenbrun’s previous films. It’s a fast-paced, enjoyable read, full of twists and jokes; like all of Schoenbrun’s work, it has a close, affectionate, reference-dense relationship to the horror genre yet contains few outright scares. The premise is now almost uncannily familiar: it is 2009, and a teenage girl, Erin Morrison, becomes obsessed with the idea of a “secret” TV channel called Public Access Afterworld, rumored to broadcast beneath the static of ordinary television. In the fall of her senior year, Erin disappears into the world of the show, pursued by her friend and occasional lover, David Sawyer. As the years go by, David pulls a wide assortment of characters into the search, uncovering the deep history of the strange world into which Erin has vanished. All the familiar elements are here: disappearing teenage girls, fantasy worlds of uncertain status, dissociation, nostalgia, obsession.

Advertisement

Schoenbrun’s films are notable for their impeccable pop cultural replicas, the accuracy of their worlds-within-worlds. The realism with which Schoenbrun depicts this fake pop culture is a crucial, destabilizing element of the experience; the false and the real weave together so tightly that it’s hard to keep hold of any meaningful difference between the two. Schoenbrun’s work demonstrates how deadening this timeless, frictionless reproduction of ephemeral culture can be (the impossibility of finding anything new to say about the millionth iteration of the Camp Miasma franchise is a running joke in Teenage Sex) while remaining attuned to the freedom it offers—the alluring promise of endless play.

As a novelist, Schoenbrun has moments of equally virtuosic world-building. The pop culture trailhead that opens into the world of Public Access Afterworld reads like a slice of gruesome Internet ephemera, something you could easily convince yourself you’d stayed up late reading about one night on Wikipedia and then forgotten:

Local weatherman Ray “Can You Say Sunshine” Davino killed himself live on air at 5:35 P.M. on September 3, 1988, on Dallas–Fort Worth ABC Channel 8 WFAA, pointing a gun at his head in the middle of the five-day forecast, rambling for forty-eight seconds in a half-coherent final monologue about the absurdity of reality, then pulling the trigger as if it was all part of his nightly routine.

This path also winds through several “forgotten” episodes of nonexistent trashy television that Schoenbrun captures with deadpan accuracy, as though tuning into the reality of a universe closely adjacent to ours:

Do you remember the TV show Short Stack?…

Short Stack was a family sitcom that aired for eight seasons on ABC from 1977 to 1985, Saturday nights at 8:30 Eastern / 7:30 Central….

Maybe you remember Lil’ Angus, the show’s breakout fan favorite character….

If you’re still drawing a blank on Short Stack, maybe this will jog your memory: “I dono about that!”

Lil Angus’s iconic catchphrase, which you had to live under a rock not to hear ten times a day during the show’s initial run.

Navigating the elaborate alternate universe of pop culture Schoenbrun has constructed is pleasurably uncanny, a bit like visiting a wax museum of the entire world.

But much of the emotional power of Schoenbrun’s filmmaking has gone missing. Instead of concentrating on a single, intense relationship, as the films do, Public Access Afterworld takes up the perspectives of several different characters, in multiple timelines. The book is presented as a series of TV “episodes” contained within a frame narrative. In the opening pages, an unnamed narrator says they heard the episodes told, “like campfire stories,” by someone going by the name David Sawyer, a fellow patient at a youth rehabilitation center who “claimed there was a fake TV show stuck inside their brain, and that they desperately needed to get it out.” And indeed, in a note included in advance copies of the book, Schoenbrun says that they initially conceived and wrote it as “1,600 pages of television screenplays,” before rewriting it as a novel when they realized that such a show would never get made. Whether this is true or another metafictional game, there is an action-packed quality to the book, a privileging of plot over character, that does over time start to feel wearying. After all, a novel is not a summary of a TV show; it has its own pleasures. Public Access Afterworld has these, too, but one has to look a bit harder to find them.

After focusing on Erin and David in the first “episode,” Schoenbrun jumps ahead to the present day and introduces Bethany Peters, “a twenty-seven-year-old trans girl playing chicken with the poverty line down in Texas,” who is employed as a content moderator for a YouTube-esque tech company called GlobalVill. The narrator declares, “Every TV show has a hero. Buffy had Buffy, Xena had Xena, and Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman had Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman. My TV show has Bethany Peters.” Bethany is special, and we know she is special, not only because the narrator tells us so but because the plot revolves around her. She has unique powers, everyone is after her, and everyone is also a little bit in love with her. As the novel progresses, its simplistic morality starts to feel like fan fiction: Bethany is the chosen one, the “receiver,” possessing an inherent specialness. She is literally “one in ten billion,” the person on whom the survival of the entire universe depends. David Sawyer, meanwhile, unable to let go of his obsessive pursuit of Erin, becomes one of the most notorious serial killers in American history and ultimately makes the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted list.

It’s almost too much—that is, until you remember that the “episodes” are being recounted by someone named David Sawyer, “the same name as one of the characters in their stories.” David the storyteller and David the character are not the same person. We know this in part because David the storyteller, the narrator implies, has transitioned (they have a new name and use they/them pronouns). David the character, however, never does. You might even say that telling this story is in part what allows David the storyteller to transition; after telling it, they get the TV show out of their head and disappear.

One way of interpreting the novel, then, is that in order to survive, David has to tell themself a story, one in which they’re divided neatly into two parts: a bad, selfish cis straight man who causes harm to the people he loves, and a heroic, beloved, too-perfect trans woman. Both the vilification of David and the idolization of Bethany have a slightly flat, unreal quality, which is what makes the story feel more like television than real life. And yet through this crack in reality something new emerges. The story serves its purpose. David the storyteller slips into a new reality, and is free.

Toward the end of the novel, Bethany wakes up in Public Access Afterworld, which takes the form of a kind of supernatural asylum. She sees, written on her door, the name “David Sawyer,” before it shifts and is replaced by her old pre-transition name. Recalling her childhood, she remembers, pre-transition, being a small boy with an “imaginary friend” named Bethany. Depressed and hospitalized, the child decides to make Bethany “real”—to become Bethany: “[Bethany] was brave and strong and resolved, just like she had always been when she was someone else’s imaginary friend. And she was beautiful. And she was real.” But in return Bethany has to exile the child, to make him as “imaginary” as Bethany once was:

As long as Bethany was alive herself, he still would be as well, scared and shattered in his childhood bedroom. So he lived with her. And now he was the imaginary one inside her head. And yet she knew he was still very real at the same time.

To create anything new, we have to pull it out of the realm of the imagination: every work of art, every invention, every new identity, every major life choice must be conceived before it can be made real. In that sense, imagination precedes reality: that is why it’s realer than real. But the relationship between the real and the imaginary is not a simple one. The boundary is porous and must be carefully patrolled.

In I Saw the TV Glow, Maddy slips into The Pink Opaque while Owen remains, suffocating and miserable, in the suburbs. He is her shadow. He is her fantasy as much as she is his—the story she tells herself about how terrible her life would have been had she never escaped. She needs him, and he needs her; they are bound together, and the tension between them is the gap (or the lake, if you will) out of which the story flows. As I walked out of the theater after seeing that movie, I remember feeling a huge wash of gratitude for my life—a life in the city, where I am free to be queer, a life where I can determine my own gender expression, a life where I am an artist. But this was followed by a strange, flickering image, almost a vision, of a life in a different reality, a life in which I had made none of those choices, in which I lived in my hometown, owned a house there, and saw my family every day.

The life I live now, which I love, has exiled that life to the realm of the imagination. By necessity, in the stories I tell, that version of myself is lonely, suffocated, and sad. Her imagined suffering helps make my real life possible. But, I wonder, if she were to catch a glimpse of my life, would she envy it? Would she think of my life as a fantasy, and try to chase it down and make it real? Or would she tell herself the kinds of stories about me that would help make her life bearable? Would I be an inspiration, or a cautionary tale?

entries.title: The Tightrope Walker
entries.summary: How did Trump manage to turn a failed coup d’état into a story of his own martyrdom?
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Had you found yourself, these past pre-midterm months, obsessively appalled by the dark signs and wonders coming out of Washington: the stunningly unqualified people elevated to high office, the systemic corruption, self-dealing, and abuse of power, the undermining of the country’s alliances, the illegal tariffs, the catastrophic war of choice in the Middle East, and on and on? You had a right to be appalled, of course, but not to be surprised. This is the president, after all, who more than five years ago exhorted his followers to stage a violent coup on national television in which at least five people died. Afterward the federal government indicted and convicted nearly 1,300 rioters who had assaulted police, ransacked the Capitol, and tried to halt the peaceful transfer of power. Those felons had acted on the public encouragement of the outgoing forty-fifth president of the United States, and he pardoned them all on the first day of his second term. Which leads to a simple question: How is it that the only president in US history to mount a coup d’état was ushered back to the White House four years later by a plurality of American voters? As we gaze in queasy fascination at the clamorous combat playing out in Washington, what does it say about the world’s most powerful state that it was unable to defend itself against such a threat? Was it somnolence, or decadence, or a simple failure of imagination?

In the bright, cold early morning of January 6, I found myself wandering the otherworldly precincts of the Washington Monument, a few hundred yards from the Ellipse, where the president was soon to speak.* It took me a moment to realize that I had stumbled into an armed camp. Bearded men in tactical vests. Guys in MAGA hats checking sidearms on their hips. A man sighting in an assault rifle. And yet had I not told friends, when they asked why I was flying to Washington for January 6, that I was “going to attend Trump’s coup”? It was a joke, but only barely. “Big protest in D.C. on January 6th,” the president had tweeted on December 19. “Be there, will be wild!” The evidence of what was to come was splashed all over the Internet. But I could not yet quite grasp what I was seeing.

By its end tens of millions of people had witnessed the brutality of that day on national television, and it is brought back to savage life in Mary Clare Jalonick’s Storm at the Capitol: An Oral History of January 6th. “I can just remember my breath catching in my throat,” recalls the Capitol Police officer Caroline Edwards,

because what I saw was just a war scene…. There were officers on the ground. You know, they were bleeding. They were throwing up. I saw friends with blood all over their faces. I was slipping in people’s blood. I was catching people as they fell. It was carnage. It was chaos. I can’t even describe what I saw.

What looked like bloody medieval chaos—and, with all the bear spray and tear gas and blood and vomit, stank like it—was in fact a uniquely postmodern coup d’état: loosely organized online with various highly adaptable moving parts, inspired by the president of the United States. Tens of thousands of Trump foot soldiers came determined to “stop the steal.” Mixed in with these loyalists, many of them armed, were more organized groups of paramilitaries who were determined, as the Oath Keepers leader Stewart Rhodes put it on January 4, to support “President Trump’s fight to defeat the enemies foreign and domestic who are attempting a coup, through the massive vote fraud and related attacks on our Republic.” This “mirror language”—we must prevent a coup (in fact, attempt a coup)—is an increasingly unavoidable feature of our age that stems from the ongoing battle over legitimacy: Who exactly was mounting the coup? The paramilitaries saw themselves as following in the footsteps of the revolutionary forces of old to prevent a coup by the Washington establishment against their rightful president. By early afternoon, Jalonick notes, they “were headed toward the Capitol.”

The coup was free form, improvisatory, adaptive—that is, very Trumpian. Evidence suggests that after his speech Trump was vaguely planning to drive to the Capitol, mount the steps, confront his vice-president directly, and persuade him by force of will to accept the slates of fake electors that had been forged and signed in the seven swing states over the past weeks, or at least to send the votes back to the state legislatures. When, despite his angry insistence, Trump’s Secret Service agents refused to take him there, he sat alone before the television in the dining room off the Oval Office and, wielding his telephone and his tweets, guided his thousands of supporters. I clearly recall the moment when, deep in the huge motley wave trooping toward the Capitol, a woman near me festooned in American flag garb bent over her phone and shrieked, “Pence has thrown us under the bus!” Jalonick’s witnesses describe the moment:

Advertisement

Jessica Watkins, US Army veteran and bar owner, Oath Keepers, Ohio: So before we left the Ellipse, like, the crowd was real, real thick. And then, like, everybody—like, literally everybody—just started pulling out their phones. They were like, “Pence betrayed us. Pence betrayed us.” Like, we have to go….

Jason Dolan, former marine, Oath Keepers, Florida: I think you kind of felt a palpable feeling where the crowd went from being pretty—a pretty happy, joyful crowd to a pretty kind of pissed-off crowd.

This dark metamorphosis was entirely owed to Trump. It was 2:24 when the president, still watching the crowd on television and perhaps having finally conceded that his coaxing and threats had failed to persuade the vice-president to “do the right thing,” tweeted, “Mike Pence didn’t have the courage to do what should have been done,” and the crowd turned very ugly. The shouts of “Hang Mike Pence!” began, and Trump was quickly informed by a panicked White House aide of the vice-president’s peril. “So what?” the president responded. Even as the crowd surged wildly through the Capitol and the vice-president and then the senators and representatives hunkered down in fear for their lives, the president was personally lobbying senators to delay certifying the election:

Sen. Mike Lee, R-UT: Moments after the proceedings in the Senate were halted by the Capitol Police, my phone rang. The caller ID indicated that the call was coming from the White House…. To my great surprise, it was…President Trump on the other end of the line….

Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-AL: When he brought me the phone, it said “White House” on it. It was the president.

Sen. Mike Rounds, R-SD: And so I was sitting here, and Coach [Tuberville] is right next to me. And the conversation…basically there’s a lobbying effort going on….

And he says, “Well, Mr. President, I gotta go. I guess they’re gonna get us out of here now.” And I never forgot that. Because while we were in the room, and there was enough going on to where they were going to remove us, there was still a lobbying effort going on by the president of the United States to stop the ballot from moving forward.

Amid the overwhelming violence at the Capitol, Trump was still single-mindedly determined to triumph over the system and remain in office.

What do you do with the perpetrator of a failed coup d’état who also happens to be president? What do you do with a chief of state who commits a crime against the state? The framers were familiar with such cases from their classical educations. They knew of Catiline, who in 63 BCE plotted to overthrow the Roman Republic and was killed battling republican troops. Had he survived, Cicero—serving as consul at the time—certainly would have had him executed. And of course they knew of Julius Caesar, whom a group of senators, in the belief that they were defending the republic, assassinated shortly after he’d named himself dictator. In both cases, a crime against the state was punished with the most severe sanction. In our own era, the little-known ex-corporal Adolf Hitler mounted the hapless Beer Hall Putsch in Munich against the Weimar Republic, served nine months in prison—he used them to dictate Mein Kampf, which became a best seller—and a decade later was named chancellor of Germany. In perhaps the closest parallel, Alberto Fujimori, who in 1992 mounted what in Peru was called an autogolpe (self-coup), was eventually imprisoned. (Peruvians recently elected his daughter president.) It is hard to think of a leader who mounted a failed coup going free only to be reelected four years later.

In this as in so many other things Donald Trump is singular. His decade at the pinnacle of our political life has been a stress test for our constitutional system and again and again has shown it to be badly wanting. If anything qualifies as the high crimes deserving of impeachment and conviction—with their accompanying banishment from high office—it was his actions on January 6. And yet the senators, having borne witness to his crimes, came ten votes short of convicting him.

Mitch McConnell, who as the Senate Republicans’ leader bears perhaps the greatest responsibility for that failure, put the matter squarely to his colleagues and the country:

There is no question—none—that President Trump is practically and morally responsible for provoking the events of the day. No question about it. The people who stormed this building believed they were acting on the wishes and instructions of their president.

He then concluded, “We have no power to convict and disqualify a former office holder who is now a private citizen.” (McConnell neglected to mention that he himself was responsible for delaying the Senate trial.) Not to worry, McConnell went on: “President Trump is still liable for everything he did while he was in office as an ordinary citizen…. He didn’t get away with anything yet. Yet. We have a criminal justice system in this country.”

Advertisement

Whether McConnell was sincere in his professed belief that the Constitution forbids the conviction of a private citizen or merely was seeking to avoid the political retribution a vote for conviction would have brought from the tens of millions of Republicans who still worshiped Trump, he had in effect, by blocking Trump’s conviction, handed the hot potato off to someone else. For that criminal justice system he praised so highly was now in the hands of President Joseph R. Biden.

Or rather in those of Biden’s attorney general, Merrick B. Garland. The incoming Democratic administration, and Garland in particular, had pledged to “depoliticize” a Justice Department that was thought to have been badly corrupted. Trump had publicly excoriated his first attorney general, Jeff Sessions, for failing to “protect” him, had summarily fired the FBI director, James Comey, for investigating what Trump called “the Russia hoax,” and had ordered that the special prosecutor named to carry out that investigation, Robert Mueller, be fired, too. These were all shocking departures from how business had been done in the Justice Department since its reconstruction after the abuses of the Nixon administration. For decades, write Carol Leonnig and Aaron C. Davis in their meticulous account, Injustice: How Politics and Fear Vanquished America’s Justice Department, veterans of the department warned young prosecutors

of Justice’s past failures to be transparent and impartial. Such violations risk undermining public confidence in the justice system….

Through the passage of decades, Justice has become a living, breathing organism of dedicated public servants yoked together to uphold these shared values in Republican and Democratic administrations. They pledged to keep Justice blind and impartial—and independent from political influence. They agreed that the facts and the law would guide their decisions on whether to charge a suspect or drop a prosecution when the evidence warranted.

Admirable words but perhaps a touch high-minded: one needn’t go back to Nixon to find persuasive instances of the Justice Department acting politically.

Still, there is no question that Garland, who had been a distinguished prosecutor and then a respected federal judge—and whom McConnell and his Republican majority refused a hearing in 2016 after Barack Obama nominated him to the Supreme Court—believed strongly in these principles. “As everyone who watched yesterday’s events in Washington now understands,” Garland said, after the president-elect introduced him on January 7, “the rule of law is not just some lawyer’s turn of phrase, it is the very foundation of our democracy.” And coming into office after Trump, how could he not be painfully aware, as Leonnig and Davis remind us, that the “department’s political independence…was never protected under law, but instead flourished through American presidents’ shared respect for this core precept”? It was these weak points in the governing structure—longtime practice dictated by norms, not laws—that Trump had been quick to sniff out and exploit. In doing so, he had left the Justice Department and the FBI skittish and politically traumatized.

By the time Garland was confirmed as attorney general in early March 2021, the Department of Justice was already fully engaged in a vast effort to prosecute the thousands who had breached the Capitol on January 6. Using cell phone data and videos posted to the Internet, hundreds of FBI agents and prosecutors identified and built cases against those who had bloodied police officers, smashed the Capitol doors and windows, and invaded the Senate and House chambers. As Garland had explained during his confirmation hearings, “We begin with the people on the ground, and we work our way up to those who are involved, and further involved, and we will pursue these leads wherever they take us.” There would be, that is, no leapfrogging to more powerful figures who actually might have planned and directed what happened that day or incited it with their ringing words to the crowd.

Garland was right that for many crimes this is standard law enforcement procedure: drug trafficking, for example. But to move against the suspected planners and directors of the coup—notably, the former president of the United States—would expose Garland’s beloved DOJ to charges that it was acting in the cause of political retribution. And did not the new attorney general, as he had said at his confirmation hearings, want “to turn down the volume on the way in which people view the department—that the Justice Department not be the center of partisan disagreement”? Investigating the former president for fomenting a coup was not exactly the way to regain the DOJ’s reputation for bipartisanship, even if the crime had been witnessed by the entire country. And it was not simply Garland’s determination to “right the ship at Justice.” The new attorney general “had told a few friends,” according to Leonnig and Davis, that he hoped that the country on January 6 “had in fact ‘burst a bubble’ of hyperpartisanship” and that in its aftermath the United States “was ready to pick up the pieces and move on, as it had after Watergate.”

For a nonpartisan attorney general this would seem a remarkably political basis on which to decline to investigate directly the author of the greatest political crime in the country’s history. Not only did the judgment prove to be strikingly ill founded, it blithely assumed that the threat to the state had passed. Whatever the reason, because of his reluctance to have the DOJ seen to be acting “politically,” Garland and his top associates proved willing essentially to put aside clear evidence that Trump, Roger Stone, Rudolph Giuliani, and others had committed crimes in trying to nullify the results of a national election—evidence that became impossible to deny once the House’s January 6th Committee began holding its hearings. And Garland was not alone. Leonnig and Davis describe how FBI investigators also proved “a little gun-shy of tangoing with Trump again.” Trump’s relentless, savage criticism of the FBI and the DOJ had had its effect. From the White House he had indefatigably worked the refs by denouncing them over “the Russia hoax,” among other things, and the refs were now unwilling to risk further provoking him.

As for higher-level officials at the FBI, many “saw the Capitol attack investigation as a political minefield if they leapt to pursue a former president or his aides at this stage.” Obviously they were right. But does it follow that both the crime against the state and its perpetrators should go uninvestigated? Going forward with an investigation, of course, was certain to sharpen the department’s own political divisions. Injustice is perhaps at its best in showing these internal political stresses as the various January 6 cases progressed. FBI agents in red states slow-walked or refused to interview witnesses or even execute arrest warrants. “On multiple occasions,” Leonnig and Davis write, “prosecutors had groused that agents had even resisted investigative steps involving members of the Proud Boys, who had helped lead the charge, breaking windows and forcing their way into the Capitol.” Elsewhere agents questioned why “grandmothers and blue-collar dads who seemed to have followed the mob” would be charged with any crime more serious than trespassing. Meanwhile Garland’s reluctance to investigate those who had led the coup was attracting critics within the department who

worried an obsession with safeguarding the perception of an apolitical DOJ was interfering with its core mission in a moment with little historical precedent. To them, the department couldn’t uphold the rule of law without bringing the most senior people responsible for January 6 to justice.

After the failed coup, was anyone who could make decisions within the federal government concerned to protect the country from its perpetrator? Acquitted in the Senate, Trump had regained his grip on the Republican Party and begun leading a campaign of retribution against members who had voted for his impeachment. Party leaders flocked to Mar-a-Lago to kiss the ring. The former president was growing more powerful by the day, with the same unmatched ability to command the news cycle at his pleasure or his whim.

Would the United States government ever have indicted the president who staged a coup against it had the House’s January 6th Committee not blazoned, in the summer of 2022, the damning evidence of his crimes all over prime-time television? Garland finally let himself be forced to select a special counsel to investigate “whether any person or entity unlawfully interfered with the transfer of power following the 2020 presidential election” only on November 18, 2022, nearly two years after Trump had staged his coup to hold on to the White House—and three days after he had declared his candidacy to retake it.

Which is to say that Garland and the Biden administration, by resisting until the last moment the effort to investigate and punish the instigators of the coup, had contrived to let the story of Trump’s struggle against prosecution and the story of his effort to recapture the White House become one story. Would the former president become the first in history to be indicted? Would he become the first to be convicted? Would he be able to delay his trial until after the election? Would he spend his next years in the White House or in the penitentiary? “That is a vastly different kind of politics,” observes Michael Wolff in All or Nothing: How Trump Recaptured America, “the man on the tightrope without a net.”

Who can take their eyes off him? As Trump’s third presidential campaign came to life…and as the stakes for him became crystal clear, his proposition as a candidate playing both hero and martyr became utterly straightforward: Elect me or destroy me.

Perhaps Trump’s greatest skill as a politician is his ability to tell stories, and the Biden administration had just given him a momentous one: the story of his martyrdom. First the powers that be had stolen the election, and now they were trying to put him in jail. It was a tale of persecution and resentment and grievance—dark emotions that his supporters broadly shared. Had they too not suffered at the hands of the nefarious elites who had shipped their jobs to China? Had not the elites thrown open the border so that illegal immigrants could steal the jobs that were left? Had not the usurper Democratic president brought terrible inflation that had stolen their savings and made their lives unaffordable? And was not Trump showing every day that he knew what it was to be unfairly harmed and hounded by the powers that be? He did know how they felt, he would tell his exultant crowds, and the only way for them to fight back was to vote for him: “They’re after you, I just happen to be standing in the way.” Or, in a piquant variation that Wolff quotes, “Our country is being destroyed, and the only thing standing between you and its obliteration is me.”

Can any election in American history match 2024 in sheer insanity? On a television debate stage in Atlanta, barely 130 days before the vote, the incumbent Democratic president collapsed into geriatric incoherence and in the days after was forced to give way to his far less well known vice-president. The Republican challenger (and former president), meanwhile, was indicted four times on federal and state felony charges, including obstructing an official proceeding and conspiring to defraud the government, and convicted in New York of thirty-four felonies tied to covering up his affair with a porn star. His unrepentant mug shot from Atlanta—he was booked there on a RICO rap for interfering in the election—became a treasured artifact of the campaign. So, too, did a Supreme Court decision, written by Chief Justice John Roberts, granting the president almost unqualified immunity for acts committed within the ambit of his official duties. The decision by the Court to intervene, together with the federal government’s two-year delay in investigating and indicting him, made it impossible to try him for the coup before the election. Would a jury have convicted him? We will never know because the American people in their wisdom went ahead and elected the defendant their forty-seventh president. The federal felony charges were withdrawn.

There are many ways to understand the 2024 election, but one begins with the perception that Trump was a former president who simply had the better story to tell. He dominated the news from what he denounced as his “Stalinist show trials,” holding impromptu press conferences in the courthouse hallways. He lost many of these cases, of course, not only the porn star case but the E. Jean Carroll defamation suits and the business fraud suits in New York, and he often seemed to go out of his way to alienate prosecutors and judges with his antics. Actually, though, Wolff reminds us, “for drama, his courtroom appearances were serving as a better debate replacement.”

He is hardly even playing the game at hand. He, and perhaps only he, is seeing a much larger game: The legal strategy is the media strategy; the media strategy is the legal strategy.

The goal is not to hide or minimize the legal peril, but to bring it on. Combine everything: It’s all part of one big witch hunt. It’s all part of one big election interference. The goal is to hammer DAs, judges, Jack Smith, and primary opponents—it’s the system against him.

Trump recognizes that every indictment juices his fundraising and raises him in the polls and that, as Wolff puts it, “he wins this trial, whatever its outcome, if he wins this election.” But it is a tightrope walk, and the over-the-shoulder point of view in this book is from some point on the rope itself. “Can you believe this shit?” Wolff quotes Trump as saying. “They are literally trying to put me in jail. That’s actually pretty cool. I’m like Nelson Mandela. I’m ready, I’ll do fine, and you send me to jail, I’m guaranteed to be president.”

The indictments, the prosecutors, the courts: all of it is a dramatic media machine, allowing him to dominate every news cycle as the heroic martyr, enacted and reenacted. “Trumpian politics is an act of cruelty,” Wolff writes. “He’s a deranged comic with a rapt audience.” The anger, the defiance, the aggression are constant, and for his aggrieved partisans both satisfying and cathartic. Trump proves, however much democracy advocates may resist admitting it, that the more powerful appeal is often to voters’ darker natures. “He rises,” writes Wolff, “in his own mind as well as in the polls, as a function of how much he can trash an opponent.” To discuss Trump in policy terms—as the candidate who won, for example, by promising to tame inflation—takes too literally what people tell pollsters, for Trump as always ran on few real policies. Wolff writes:

Trump is often just a raw nerve, his own rage, resentments, and personal grievances churning in him and, at any given moment, expressed in his public performances—which is exactly what makes them so compelling and, for the campaign, unpredictable,

The suspense of unpredictability is at the heart of much drama and entertainment, and if the reign of Trump proves anything it is that much of politics, no matter how serious, begins with being unable to look away.

What was true of the campaign, of course, is true of his second presidency. More so, really, because that “raw nerve,” as Trump ages, becomes steadily more visible—indeed, more obtrusive. One is struck once again, in Wolff’s close portrait of Trump regaining the presidency, by how unsuited he is to occupy the office. He is an aberrant pile of instincts and impulses, which largely help him command the fascinated or appalled stares of tens of millions. “He’s just a content machine,” as Senator Chris Murphy put it. “He’s creating an episode every day that you have to tune in to.” These episodes shape the public conversation, however rage filled or erratic or inane and however little they have to do with the national interest. Meanwhile his waning popularity did not stop his grift or his corruption or even much constrain his ability to dominate the supine and still largely terrified Republicans. Sinking poll numbers or not, Trump remains, as Wolff writes,

the truly consummate huckster, unafraid that his misrepresentations might be revealed because he had, up his sleeve, endlessly more of them. Without humility, and with a taste—even a need—for constant battle, he never relented, never even came close to an admission, and hence a true, no less final reckoning always rolled into the future.

Nearly two years later, has that reckoning finally come? For many once willing to support Trump, the act had grown old. Unending tumult could no longer mask high prices and endless war. He had run as a populist but he governed as a gilded, royalist authoritarian, and people struggling to get by noticed. Young people, Latinos, and Blacks watched him break his promises of lower prices and no new wars and abandoned him and his antics in disgust.

Now the consummate huckster has two more years in power. Will he let himself fade into the background, puttering around his ballroom and his grand triumphal arch, or will he charge once again onto center stage to “fight, fight, fight”? Will his unquenchable narcissism permit him to share credit and attention and actually get things done? In the end that man on the tightrope—we have seen this before—will do anything to keep the spotlight fixed only on him.

A longer version of this article appears in Crossing the Rubicon: The Betrayal of American Democracy, 2000–2026, just published by New York Review Books.

entries.title: Interview with a Bandit
entries.summary: Many Nigerians have turned to violence after years of suffering under widespread government corruption.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Were it not for his AK-47, you wouldn’t think Babangida—a lanky, dark-skinned, soft-spoken man in his late thirties, wearing a traditional caftan and a colorful cloth cap—was the type to harm anyone. Yet he is one of some 30,000 gunmen, known locally as “bandits,” who for the past fifteen years have terrorized a huge swath of Nigeria’s countryside, from the dusty villages of the state of Sokoto in the northwest to the lush farmlands of the state of Benue in the central region. Without warning, gangs of them—some with just a dozen or so members, others with hundreds—swoop into towns and villages on motorcycles, loot and destroy property, and kill or kidnap people for ransom. Thousands have lost their lives in the mayhem, and hundreds of thousands have fled their homes to escape it.

After months of negotiation, Babangida agreed to an interview with one of us, the Agence France-Presse journalist Aminu Abubakar, in a remote village in his home state of Katsina, in the country’s northwest. The village lies down an unpaved track, far from the highway. Its few hundred inhabitants live in mud huts with grass-thatched roofs, amid baobab, acacia, and neem trees. In the surrounding fields they grow corn, sorghum, and other crops and keep goats, chickens, and cows. They get around mostly by bike, motorcycle, and oxcart. No one owns a car.

Last December, in what President Donald Trump called a “Christmas present,” Washington launched air strikes on Sokoto, claiming to combat what US lawmakers and evangelical groups have called a genocide against Christians committed by bandits, most of whom are Muslim, and by other armed groups, including the Islamic State. The US, alleging violations of religious freedom, put Nigeria on a watch list of Countries of Particular Concern. The Christian genocide claim is highly dubious: most of the bandits’ victims have been Muslims, not Christians, and only about 5 percent of violence against civilians has targeted Christians for their faith, according to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a respected monitoring group. But when experts try to explain what is actually going on, they tend to cite a vague array of social, economic, and political factors, including historical grievances, climate change, weak governance, and resource scarcity, none of which points to straightforward policy solutions.

Upon hearing US lawmakers characterize the bandits as Islamist fanatics, a Nigerian government conflict mediator who had befriended Babangida urged him to tell his side of the story to the world, which is how he came to speak with Aminu. Throughout the interview, he gripped his AK-47, its barrel pointed to the sky. He had been a bandit for nearly a decade but said he didn’t know how many raids he’d participated in or how many people he’d kidnapped or killed. “We don’t keep records,” he said. But “no bandit just picked up a gun overnight and turned to violence. There is always a story behind it. Let me tell you mine.”

Born in 1988 into a family of Fulani pastoralists, Babangida grew up in a village even more remote than the one where Aminu met him. It had no school, no clinic, no running water, no electricity, and virtually no other modern amenity. His family was not rich; they had about a hundred cows, whereas some had thousands. But they managed to eke out a living by subsistence farming and selling milk.

As a child, Babangida and the other village boys would typically rise early and take their families’ animals out to the fields for grazing, then return in the late afternoon. They would bring along some millet gruel and water, a stick for prodding the cattle, a machete for cutting tall grass, and a transistor radio to listen to music and the news. His most vivid childhood memory is of his circumcision at age seven. Neighbors and relatives gave the boy a flock of chickens. His family feasted on some of them right away and sold the rest to buy a goat, which Babangida raised. He married at eighteen, and after his first child was born the following year, his family gave him a bull and two heifers, which he bred while continuing to help out with his family’s herds.

Every year, with the approach of the dry season, Babangida’s family and thousands of others headed south with their animals in search of pasture and returned in time for planting. This custom—known as the transhumance—has been shaped by centuries of adaptation to one of the world’s harshest environments. It usually lasts for months and may cover hundreds of miles. The herders are seeking water during the dry season and escaping the Harmattan winds, which blow down from the Sahara, causing dust storms that reduce visibility to a few meters and sometimes send haze across the ocean to Florida.* The herder migration routes avoid the breeding grounds of the sleeping sickness–carrying tsetse fly, which swarms from the Sahara’s edge to the southern forests with the rains, and they follow the growth of fodder that produces the best milk. Acacia tree leaves, for example, which goats love, are 20 percent protein, and baobab leaves have fifteen times as much calcium per gram as milk does.

This was the only life Babangida knew. He expected that one day he’d have his own herd and become independent. But ecological and social forces that had been gathering for at least a decade before he was born soon shattered this modest dream.

In the past, herders tended to arrive in the southern farming regions in time for the cows to eat the stubble in the fields and fertilize them for the next planting season—an arrangement that worked for everyone. But since the droughts of the 1970s the transhumance has been pushed farther south. Meanwhile the sedentary population has grown and farms have spread into areas designated by the government in the 1960s as grazing reserves. Local officials, including village chiefs, police, and even the military, have done little to stop farmers from encroaching into grazing areas, and some have colluded with them. Now herders might pass through a grazing area on their way south only to find it under cultivation on the way back, Babangida said. They have no choice but to herd their animals through the new crop rows, causing quarrels with angry farmers that over the years have become increasingly protracted and violent.

Farmer–herder conflicts are not new in this part of the world, but they were rarer in the past and were usually resolved by elders from both sides who constituted an informal justice system largely invisible to Nigeria’s colonial occupiers and coup-prone postindependence governments. Fulani elders, known as ardos, would accompany the transhumance and form relationships of mutual aid with other ardos and farmer elders along the way, negotiating fair compensation for lost animals or crops. But these days Fulani elders are far less likely to accompany the transhumance, preferring to engage in sedentary—and safer—activities like farming or preaching the Quran. Commercialization has also weakened the delicate diplomacy that sustained the transhumance for thousands of years. Today young herders increasingly work for investors, government officials, or wealthy agriculturalists rather than their own families. When conflicts over trampled crops arise, these herders are more likely to try to pay off the farmers rather than rely on long-standing relationships among elders to negotiate and maintain harmony, says the West Africa expert Matthew Turner.

As traditional justice mechanisms eroded, the government failed to fill the vacuum, and sometimes made things worse. Nigeria’s police are notoriously corrupt and often biased against herders, a subject Babangida was eager to discuss. “Say a herder destroys a piece of a farmer’s field,” he explained.

The village chief will set the fine well beyond the value of the crops destroyed. But when a farmer kills a herder’s cattle, it’s declared the herder’s fault and he receives no compensation. If the chief calls the police, they will connive with a judge to raise the fine even more, so the herder is wiped out. If the farmer was injured or killed, all hell breaks loose and the chief, police, and judge make fortunes out of us.

One reason for this perceived anti-Fulani bias is that it is usually farmers from the communities where the police are stationed who initiate complaints about their trampled fields. Fulani pastoralists have also long been looked down upon as backward and uncivilized by the sedentary people of northern Nigeria, most of whom belong to the Hausa ethnic group. The supposedly hapless Fulani are the butt of endless Hausa jokes, and you can sense their injured pride in their terse and taciturn demeanors.

Another problem is that the police, woefully under-resourced like virtually all public services in Nigeria, frequently collude with brutal vigilante squads made up of volunteers from local farming communities. These militias, formed as a response to banditry by Fulani herders, have been portrayed in the media as informal peacekeepers, but to the Fulani they are a terrifying scourge responsible for wanton attacks on farmsteads, cattle rustling, and even murder. It was a series of such attacks that changed Babangida’s life and that of his community forever.

“One night,” Babangida said, “our village was invaded by vigilantes, [who were] assisted by police. They broke into our home, arrested my mother and younger brother, and took ninety-seven cattle”—nearly all they owned. Babangida had no idea why his family was targeted. It may have been retribution for alleged offenses carried out by other Fulani or just theft.

For the Fulani, cows are not mere material possessions. Each one has a name, and wherever they wander, the lead cow always knows her way home. Stolen cows will sometimes grunt and pull at their ropes when their true owners come searching for them in a crowded market—even before their owners recognize them. Some thieves have even been caught this way.

Babangida’s family was not so lucky:

We finally found the cows in Gusau [a city in the neighboring state of Zamfara]. The police demanded 1.8 million naira [about $1,300] to bail my mother and brother out. Eventually we managed to get ten of our cows back too, but I sold them to buy guns, one of which I’m holding now.

He didn’t know where it came from: “If you have money, suppliers will bring guns to your doorstep.”

Babangida and his family moved to a bandit community in the forest. “Our cattle were gone,” he said; his life as a herder was over. He knows of many other Fulani who were pushed into banditry this way:

The same policeman who took our herd stole 480 cows and 300 goats from another herder. After lengthy court proceedings, he was given a few animals back, but the case has been transferred to a higher court and there is no information about the animals he lost.

The parents of a young woman he knows set out on a trip to inform relatives about her upcoming wedding. Their bus was flagged down at a vigilante checkpoint. Because they were Fulani, they were singled out, pinned to the ground, and slaughtered. “A vigilante doesn’t verify who is a criminal and who is not,” Babangida said. “If you are Fulani, he just slits your throat when he gets you.”

“The son of that couple who were killed had a baby,” he went on.

He took five cows to the market to raise money for the naming ceremony, but when he arrived, he was arrested on suspicion that they’d been stolen. He was never a thief, and those cows were his, but his family had to sell more cows to get him released, and the original five were never returned. The naming ceremony and his sister’s wedding were still pending, so he took another seven cows to another market, where he was arrested yet again and the cows seized. More cows were sold to get him released, but the original seven were never returned.

Some of this man’s friends were bandits, and they pressured him to join them. At first he resisted, but he eventually gave in and the share he got from looting, plus contributions from other bandits, enabled him to pay for the wedding and the naming ceremony. He is now a bandit commander.

Five years ago vigilantes claiming to be smoking out bandits stormed the settlement of another of Babangida’s kinsmen and left with six hundred cows. “Two of his brothers were killed, but he managed to hide in a disused water tunnel attached to a military outpost. His parents disappeared that day, never to be seen again. One day, while searching for them in a nearby village on a market day, he was introduced to Dogo Gide,” a notorious bandit with ties to Ansaru, an al-Qaeda affiliate. Dogo Gide trained him to use a gun and then sent him to a subsidiary camp, where he now leads a kidnapping-for-ransom team.

President Trump’s claims of a Christian genocide puzzled Babangida: “Most of our victims are Muslims of the Hausa ethnic group, not Christians.” He admitted that “some bandits say they are waging jihad or striving for the sake of Allah,” and others collaborate with groups like al-Qaeda for strategic reasons. But for most bandits, “it is all about making money and revenge.”

“Years of injustices are what pushed Fulani herders into banditry,” he went on.

We were never criminals before. Wherever you see indiscriminate killings and destruction it is usually a revenge attack against other killings. Yes, the people we attack and kidnap have nothing to do with what happened to us, but the ones who robbed us are doing the same thing.

Today older bandits are being replaced by a younger generation that relies for courage on drugs—marijuana, diazepam, tramadol, codeine, whatever is cheap and easy to obtain. Stoned young bandits can become so savage that they sometimes kill hostages even after ransom is paid. Babangida and the other older bandits are terrified of them.

In the past fifteen years Nigeria has spent some $44 billion battling armed groups, including bandits, with little to show for its efforts. The army has launched air strikes on militant hideouts, set up roadblocks, and tried to cut off bandit communications. This has resulted in many bandit deaths and arrests but no reduction in attacks. In February Washington sent some two hundred soldiers to assist the Nigerian military fighting armed groups in northern Nigeria. But the violence only increased, and they were withdrawn in September.

In 2019 the Nigerian federal government announced that it would spend some $300 million to create ranches that would provide herding settlements with grazing facilities. The funding and political leadership did not materialize, and the project was roiled with controversy because locals fear any development that would lead to permanent herder settlements near their villages and farms, and they also wanted to see justice and the return of displaced people, not ranches for those they perceive as their tormentors. The government revived the scheme in August, but because of rainfall variability, the ranches will have to be enormous for it to work.

Local government officials have also tried to negotiate with bandits, offering amnesty as well as improved schools and hospitals if they lay down their guns. But these deals usually collapse, Babangida said, because the government fails to deliver on its promises.

For example, under the terms of a peace agreement in the state of Katsina, a school for herder children was built but was then converted into a military barracks. A former governor also provided funds to help bandits find another trade, but his officials stole the money. The governor then announced that any bandit without a herd would be given a bull and a cow. The funds were disbursed, but not a single Fulani got anything. Eventually any repentant bandits returned to their guns.

Bandits and vigilantes are not the only ones responsible for violence in Nigeria. The country is also beset with armed robberies, kidnappings, extrajudicial and ritual killings, secessionist agitation, and attacks by so-called unknown gunmen, whom everyone knows but is afraid to name. On Nigeria’s university campuses, gangs with names like Black Axe and Second Sons of Satan stockpile weapons, fight rival gangs, initiate new members through rape, and burn the cars of professors who don’t give them good grades.

Like Babangida, many experts attribute this chaos to injustices resulting from government corruption that force people to feel they must take matters into their own hands. Corruption exists everywhere, but as the late historian of Africa Stephen Ellis argues in This Present Darkness: A History of Nigerian Organized Crime (2016), Nigeria has long seemed like a special case.

West Africans call it “stomach infrastructure” or “the politics of the belly,” and it takes countless forms, including the embezzlement and looting of Treasury funds, vote buying, electoral fraud, kickbacks from artificially inflated government contracts, ghost workers, petty bribery of police, judges, and other government officials, tribalism, and nepotism. Nigeria is Africa’s third-richest country, but because of corruption, many of its public clinics and schools barely function. This helps explain why in the northern region, where Babangida lives and where banditry is most common, nearly 20 percent of children die by age five and only a third of adults can read.

Why is corruption so entrenched in Nigeria and so many other African countries? It’s not as though no one’s aware of it. The continent’s militaries often launch coups on the pretext of fighting corruption; the struggle for democracy is justified in the same way. Both jihadist and fundamentalist Christian movements across Africa claim the same anticorruption mission. Even Babangida sees himself as fighting for law and order.

Like nearly every Nigerian head of state before him, President Bola Tinubu campaigned on an anticorruption platform. Once in office, he sacked some corrupt officials and hired as his national security adviser Nuhu Ribadu, who was honored by the World Bank for his heroic anticorruption work. Tinubu also unveiled a justice reform program designed to reduce official corruption and speed up the resolution of cases, although implementation may take decades, and so far ordinary Nigerians have seen little change.

But President Tinubu’s government has also given lucrative contracts to his business associates and his own family members, and he appointed as Nigeria’s minister of budget and economic planning Abubakar Atiku Bagudu, a former state governor linked to the predatory Nigerian dictator Sani Abacha, who stole billions from the Treasury in the 1990s. In 2025 Ribadu was reported to have secretly paid bandit groups and Boko Haram millions of dollars in ransom—in contravention of a 2022 Nigerian law against such payments, which have been shown to increase incentives for kidnapping—in order to secure the release of hundreds of hostages.

Perhaps Nigeria’s struggle with corruption, and the violence that appears to be linked to it, has something to do with the pace at which it has been forced to modernize. In an insightful 1999 essay, the anthropologist Jean-Pierre Olivier de Sardan suggested that colonialism imposed a weak Western-style bureaucratic system—which officially condemns corruption but does virtually nothing about it—on top of strong and long-standing social networks of mutual aid that all but obligate people in power to take advantage of enrichment opportunities and share their good fortune with kin. In other words, everyone hates corruption, but those in power would be shunned by their relatives as selfish if they didn’t engage in it.

Chinua Achebe saw it coming at independence. In his novel No Longer at Ease (1960), an idealistic, Western-educated government office worker in Lagos finds himself deep in debt as a result of the mounting demands of his family and the elders in his home village who paid for his European education. Despite his lofty moral convictions, he accepts a hefty bribe and is arrested. This helps explain how corruption can be so ubiquitous, though everyone—even bandits like Babangida—complains about it day and night. Ultimately, Babangida said, “justice is the only way out. When justice is upheld, everyone will live in peace.” No doubt many in Nigeria, including his victims and their avenging vigilantes, would agree.
